19	**Matter:** Employee Handbook Compliance Review --- Colorado Employment Law Requirements
20	
21	**Matter Context and Scope**
22	
23	This checklist has been prepared in connection with the ongoing compliance review of the Oakridge Senior Living, Inc. employee handbook. The current version of the handbook is dated March 14, 2025, comprises forty-seven (47) pages across fourteen (14) sections, and was originally created in June 2019 using a Compliance Blueprint Solutions template. The handbook has been periodically updated by Denise Kowalski, Part-Time General Counsel for Oakridge Senior Living, Inc. The target distribution date for the revised and compliant handbook is August 1, 2025.
24	
25	**Company Profile Summary**
26	
27	Oakridge Senior Living, Inc. (\"Oakridge\" or the \"Company\") is a Colorado-based operator of assisted living and memory care facilities. As of April 30, 2025, the Company employs a total of six hundred twelve (612) employees, distributed as follows: three hundred eighty-nine (389) hourly non-exempt employees, one hundred forty-eight (148) salaried exempt employees, and seventy-five (75) salaried non-exempt employees. The Company operates seven (7) facilities across the state of Colorado, located in Colorado Springs, Denver, Boulder, Fort Collins, Pueblo, Grand Junction, and Durango. For fiscal year 2024, the Company reported annual revenue of approximately \$68.4 million. The Company\'s current operational footprint reflects significant recent growth: Oakridge expanded from three (3) to seven (7) facilities through the acquisition of Peak Vista Elder Care LLC (closed January 15, 2024) and Western Slope Senior Services Inc. (closed June 3, 2024). This growth trajectory is relevant to the compliance review, as the acquired facilities\' employees were transitioned onto Oakridge\'s existing policies and handbook, which may not have been updated to account for the expanded workforce or operational changes associated with the acquisitions.
28	
29	**Purpose Statement**
30	
31	This checklist identifies the key Colorado employment law requirements that must be reflected in the Oakridge Senior Living, Inc. employee handbook. It is organized by topic area and provides statutory citations, effective dates, and applicable thresholds for each requirement. It is intended to serve as the state-law benchmark for the compliance gap analysis that Briarstone & Lyle LLP will conduct by comparing this checklist against the current handbook. This checklist does not constitute a comprehensive treatise on all Colorado employment laws; rather, it focuses on the provisions most commonly addressed in employee handbooks and most relevant to Oakridge\'s operations as a healthcare and senior living employer with 612 employees across seven Colorado locations.
32	
33	Right-click to update Table of Contents
34	
35	**[Section 1: Wage and Hour Requirements]{.underline}**
36	
37	This section addresses Colorado\'s principal wage and hour requirements as they apply to Oakridge Senior Living, Inc. These requirements are primarily governed by the Colorado Overtime and Minimum Pay Standards Order Number 39 (\"COMPS Order #39\"), codified at 7 CCR 1103-1, and the Colorado Wage Claim Act, C.R.S. § 8-4-101 *et seq.* Given that the vast majority of Oakridge\'s workforce consists of hourly non-exempt and salaried non-exempt employees (464 out of 612 total employees), wage and hour compliance is a critical area for the handbook review.
38	
39	**[1.1 Minimum Wage]{.underline}**
40	
41	Colorado\'s minimum wage for calendar year 2025 is **\$14.81 per hour**, effective January 1, 2025. This rate is established pursuant to C.R.S. § 8-6-109 and is reflected in COMPS Order #39, which governs minimum wage and overtime standards for covered Colorado employees.
42	
43	Under Colorado law, the state minimum wage adjusts annually based on changes to the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (\"CPI-U\") for the Denver-Aurora-Lakewood metropolitan statistical area. The Colorado Department of Labor and Employment (\"CDLE\") publishes the adjusted rate each fall, with the new rate taking effect on January 1 of the following year. As a result, employers must review and, if necessary, update their policies and handbook provisions referencing a specific minimum wage figure on an annual basis to ensure continued compliance.
44	
45	Colorado\'s minimum wage significantly exceeds the federal minimum wage, which remains at \$7.25 per hour under the Fair Labor Standards Act (\"FLSA\"), 29 U.S.C. § 206(a)(1). Because Colorado\'s minimum wage is higher than the federal rate, the state rate controls for all employees performing work within the state of Colorado. All of Oakridge\'s seven facilities are located within Colorado, and accordingly, the \$14.81 per hour state minimum wage applies to the Company\'s entire workforce.
46	
47	Colorado law does permit a tip credit that allows employers of tipped employees to pay a lower direct cash wage, provided that the employee\'s tips bring total compensation to at least the full minimum wage. However, the tip credit is relevant primarily to the restaurant and hospitality industries. Given that Oakridge operates assisted living and memory care facilities and does not employ tipped workers in its healthcare operations, the tip credit provision is not applicable to the Company\'s workforce and need not be addressed in the handbook.
48	
49	Any handbook provision that references a specific dollar-amount wage floor must ensure that the stated amount meets or exceeds the current Colorado minimum wage of \$14.81 per hour. Any handbook provision referencing a specific wage floor below \$14.81 per hour is non-compliant as of January 1, 2025. During the handbook review, counsel should verify that any stated minimum starting wage, base pay rate, or wage floor in the handbook is at or above \$14.81 per hour and should recommend that the handbook either reference the \"then-current Colorado minimum wage\" (without specifying a dollar amount) or include a mechanism for annual updates to any stated figure.
50	
51	**[1.2 Overtime]{.underline}**
52	
53	Colorado\'s overtime requirements are governed by COMPS Order #39, 7 CCR 1103-1, Rule 4.1, and C.R.S. § 8-12-103. These provisions establish the overtime compensation obligations for covered Colorado employers and employees. Oakridge\'s healthcare and senior living operations fall squarely within the industries covered by COMPS Order #39, and accordingly, all non-exempt Oakridge employees are subject to the Colorado overtime rules set forth below.
54	
55	Under COMPS Order #39, overtime compensation is payable at one and one-half times (1.5×) the employee\'s regular rate of pay for hours worked in excess of either of the following thresholds, whichever is triggered first:
56	
57	> \(a\) **Forty (40) hours in a single workweek**; or
58	>
59	> \(b\) **Twelve (12) hours in a single workday**.
60	
61	The dual-trigger nature of Colorado\'s overtime rule is a critical distinction from federal law. Under the FLSA, overtime is triggered only by hours worked in excess of forty (40) in a workweek; the FLSA does not impose a daily overtime threshold. Colorado\'s COMPS Order #39, by contrast, requires overtime compensation when an employee works more than twelve (12) hours in any single workday, regardless of whether the employee\'s total hours for the workweek exceed forty. This means that in Colorado, an employee who works a single thirteen-hour shift is entitled to one hour of overtime pay for that day, even if the employee works fewer than forty total hours during the workweek.
62	
63	This daily overtime rule is a frequently overlooked requirement, particularly for healthcare employers that utilize twelve-hour shift schedules. In the senior living and healthcare industry, twelve-hour shifts are common, especially for certified nursing assistants (\"CNAs\"), licensed practical nurses (\"LPNs\"), registered nurses (\"RNs\"), and other direct-care staff. Oakridge should be particularly attentive to this requirement given the likelihood that many of its facility-based employees work twelve-hour or longer shifts. Any shift that extends beyond twelve hours --- whether due to scheduling, patient emergencies, shift handover delays, or mandatory overtime --- triggers the daily overtime obligation.
64	
65	The employer\'s handbook must clearly communicate **both** the weekly and daily overtime thresholds to all non-exempt employees. A handbook that references only the forty-hour weekly overtime threshold without also disclosing the twelve-hour daily overtime threshold does not adequately inform employees of their rights under Colorado law and may create compliance exposure. During the handbook review, counsel should verify that the overtime policy section of the handbook identifies both overtime triggers and explains that overtime is payable when either threshold is exceeded.
66	
67	Additionally, the handbook should address or cross-reference the Company\'s timekeeping policies to ensure that daily hours worked are accurately recorded, as this data is essential for calculating daily overtime obligations.
68	
69	**[1.3 Meal Breaks]{.underline}**
70	
71	Under COMPS Order #39, Rule 5.1, codified at 7 CCR 1103-1, employers are required to provide employees with a **thirty (30)-minute uninterrupted, duty-free meal period** when the employee works a shift of **five (5) or more hours**. This is a mandatory obligation, not a discretionary benefit. The meal break obligation is triggered at five hours, not six or eight hours.
72	
73	The meal period must be completely duty-free. During the meal period, the employee must be fully relieved of all duties and free to use the time for personal purposes, including leaving the employer\'s premises. If the nature of the work prevents the employee from being completely relieved of duties during the meal period --- for example, if a CNA or nurse must remain available to respond to patient needs --- then the meal period is not duty-free, and the employer must compensate the employee for the entire meal period as hours worked.
74	
75	Employees may waive the meal period only under specific, limited conditions permitted by COMPS Order #39. A waiver is permissible only when it is made by mutual written agreement between the employer and employee and only when the nature of the work prevents the employee from being relieved of all duties. The waiver must be voluntary; an employer may not unilaterally decide to skip or shorten meal periods.
76	
77	For healthcare employers such as Oakridge, the duty-free requirement presents particular operational challenges, as direct-care staff may be required to remain on-call or responsive to patient needs during meal periods. The handbook should clearly address the circumstances under which a meal period is considered duty-free versus compensable and should describe the process for documenting meal period waivers where applicable.
78	
79	During the handbook review, counsel should verify that the handbook\'s meal break trigger threshold matches the five-hour requirement established by COMPS Order #39, Rule 5.1. Any handbook provision that sets the meal break trigger at a threshold higher than five hours --- such as six hours or eight hours --- is non-compliant with Colorado law and must be corrected.
80	
81	**[1.4 Rest Breaks]{.underline}**
82	
83	Under COMPS Order #39, Rule 5.2, codified at 7 CCR 1103-1, Colorado employers **must** provide employees with a **paid ten (10)-minute rest break for every four (4) hours of work**, or major fraction thereof (i.e., any period of more than two hours). Rest breaks under Colorado law are **mandatory**, not discretionary. They are a legal entitlement, not a voluntary benefit that the employer may offer or withhold at its convenience.
84	
85	Rest breaks must be paid time. They cannot be deducted from the employee\'s compensable hours, and employees cannot be required to clock out for rest breaks. The cost of rest break time is borne by the employer as part of the employee\'s regular compensation.
86	
87	In practical application, the rest break entitlement operates as follows:
88	
89	> • An employee working a standard **eight (8)-hour shift** is entitled to **two (2) paid ten-minute rest breaks** --- one during the first four-hour period and one during the second four-hour period.
90	>
91	> • An employee working a **twelve (12)-hour shift** is entitled to **three (3) paid ten-minute rest breaks** --- one for each four-hour segment of the shift.
92	>
93	> • An employee working a **six (6)-hour shift** is entitled to **two (2) paid ten-minute rest breaks** --- one for the first four hours and one for the remaining two-plus hours (which constitutes a \"major fraction\" of four hours).
94	
95	The mandatory nature of rest breaks under Colorado law cannot be overstated. Any handbook language suggesting that rest breaks are optional, voluntary, \"encouraged,\" at the employer\'s discretion, or subject to operational needs is non-compliant with COMPS Order #39. The handbook must clearly state that rest breaks are mandatory and paid. While the employer retains the right to schedule the timing of rest breaks within the applicable work period to accommodate operational needs, the employer may not eliminate or deny rest breaks altogether.
96	
97	During the handbook review, counsel should examine the rest break policy carefully for any language that characterizes rest breaks as discretionary, voluntary, or \"encouraged but not required.\" Such language directly conflicts with the mandatory nature of the rest break obligation under Colorado law and must be revised to reflect that rest breaks are required by law and must be provided to all non-exempt employees.
98	
99	**[1.5 Pay Frequency and Pay Statements]{.underline}**
100	
101	Colorado law permits employers to pay employees on various pay schedules, including weekly, biweekly, semi-monthly, or monthly, as set forth in C.R.S. § 8-4-103. The employer must establish a regular payday and must pay wages on the designated schedule. Biweekly pay is a permissible and commonly used pay frequency in Colorado, and its use does not, in itself, present a compliance concern.
102	
103	In addition to timely payment, Colorado employers are required to provide itemized pay statements (commonly referred to as pay stubs or wage statements) with each wage payment. Pay statements must include, at a minimum, the employee\'s gross wages, an itemization of all deductions, net pay, and, for non-exempt employees, the total hours worked during the pay period. These requirements ensure transparency and enable employees to verify the accuracy of their compensation.
104	
105	During the handbook review, counsel should verify that the handbook accurately describes the Company\'s pay frequency and references the employee\'s right to receive an itemized pay statement with each paycheck. While the specific pay frequency used by Oakridge (biweekly) is permissible, the handbook should clearly identify the regular payday schedule so that employees understand when to expect payment.
106	
107	**[Section 2: Leave Requirements]{.underline}**
108	
109	This section addresses Colorado\'s statutory leave requirements, including the Healthy Families and Workplaces Act (\"HFWA\"), the Colorado Paid Family and Medical Leave Insurance Act (\"FAMLI\"), and the federal Family and Medical Leave Act (\"FMLA\"). As a healthcare employer with a large and diverse workforce, Oakridge must ensure that its handbook accurately reflects the full range of leave entitlements available to its employees under both state and federal law.
110	
111	**[2.1 Colorado Healthy Families and Workplaces Act (HFWA) --- Paid Sick Leave]{.underline}**
112	
113	The Colorado Healthy Families and Workplaces Act (\"HFWA\"), codified at C.R.S. § 8-13.3-401 *et seq.*, requires all Colorado employers to provide paid sick leave to their employees. The HFWA\'s paid sick leave requirements became effective on January 1, 2021 for all employers, regardless of size.
114	
115	**Accrual Rate.** Under the HFWA, employees accrue paid sick leave at a rate of **one (1) hour of paid sick leave for every thirty (30) hours worked**. This 1:30 accrual ratio is the statutory minimum and applies to all employees, including full-time, part-time, and temporary employees. The accrual obligation commences on the employee\'s first day of employment; there is no waiting period before accrual begins.
116	
117	**Annual Accrual and Use Cap.** Employers may cap the total amount of paid sick leave that an employee accrues in a given benefit year at **forty-eight (48) hours**. However, this cap applies only to total annual accrual; the employer must maintain the 1:30 accrual rate throughout the year until the cap is reached. Similarly, employers may limit the amount of paid sick leave an employee may use in a single benefit year to forty-eight (48) hours. Employees must be permitted to carry over unused accrued sick leave from one benefit year to the next, although the employer may cap total accrued balances at forty-eight (48) hours at any given time.
118	
119	**Covered Employees.** The HFWA applies to all employees working in Colorado, without exception. There is no minimum-hours or length-of-service requirement for eligibility. Part-time employees, temporary employees, per diem employees, and seasonal employees all accrue paid sick leave from their first day of work.
120	
121	**Permitted Uses.** Employees may use accrued paid sick leave for the following purposes: (i) the employee\'s own mental or physical illness, injury, or health condition, including preventive care and diagnosis; (ii) caring for a family member with a mental or physical illness, injury, or health condition; (iii) circumstances arising from a public health emergency, including quarantine, isolation, or closure of a child\'s school or place of care; (iv) circumstances related to domestic violence, sexual assault, or criminal harassment of the employee or a family member; and (v) bereavement following the death of a family member, including attending a funeral, making arrangements necessitated by the death, and grieving.
122	
123	**Combined PTO Banks.** If an employer uses a combined Paid Time Off (\"PTO\") bank --- rather than maintaining separate sick leave and vacation leave banks --- the PTO bank must at minimum satisfy the HFWA\'s accrual rate and usage requirements. Specifically, the combined PTO bank must accrue at a rate of no less than one (1) hour for every thirty (30) hours worked, and the PTO must be available for use for all HFWA-qualifying purposes listed above. An employer may not restrict the use of PTO bank hours to vacation purposes only if the PTO bank is serving as the employer\'s HFWA-compliant sick leave vehicle.
124	
125	**Handbook Review Note.** During the handbook review, counsel should verify that the handbook\'s PTO or sick leave accrual rate is at least one (1) hour for every thirty (30) hours worked. An accrual rate lower than 1:30 --- for example, one (1) hour of PTO for every forty (40) hours worked --- does not meet the statutory minimum and renders the employer\'s sick leave policy non-compliant with the HFWA. Counsel should also verify that the handbook identifies all HFWA-qualifying uses, particularly bereavement and domestic violence leave, which are sometimes omitted from older handbook templates.
126	
127	**[2.2 HFWA --- Public Health Emergency Leave (PHEL)]{.underline}**
128	
129	In addition to the accrued paid sick leave described in Section 2.1 above, the Healthy Families and Workplaces Act requires employers to provide supplemental **Public Health Emergency Leave (\"PHEL\")** when a public health emergency is declared by a federal, state, or local official. The PHEL requirement is codified at C.R.S. § 8-13.3-405 and represents a separate and additional leave entitlement beyond the employee\'s accrued sick leave balance.
130	
131	**PHEL Entitlement.** Upon the declaration of a public health emergency, employers must immediately make available up to **eighty (80) hours** of supplemental PHEL for full-time employees. For part-time employees, the PHEL entitlement is prorated based on the employee\'s average number of hours worked per week over the two-week period immediately preceding the declaration of the public health emergency. PHEL is available immediately upon declaration of the public health emergency; there is no accrual requirement, waiting period, or length-of-service prerequisite.
132	
133	**Relationship to Accrued Sick Leave.** PHEL is provided **in addition to**, and not concurrently with, the employee\'s accrued paid sick leave. An employer may not require an employee to exhaust accrued paid sick leave before using PHEL, nor may an employer reduce an employee\'s accrued sick leave balance in lieu of providing PHEL. The two entitlements are separate and cumulative.
134	
135	**Permitted Uses During a Public Health Emergency.** Employees may use PHEL for the following qualifying reasons: (i) self-quarantine or isolation due to exposure to or symptoms of the communicable illness that is the subject of the public health emergency; (ii) seeking medical diagnosis, treatment, or care for symptoms of the communicable illness; (iii) caring for a family member who is self-quarantining, isolating, or seeking medical attention; (iv) a child\'s school or childcare facility closure due to the public health emergency; (v) inability to work because the employee has a health condition that increases susceptibility to the communicable illness; and (vi) other qualifying reasons related to the public health emergency as specified by the CDLE.
136	
137	**Handbook Requirement.** The employer\'s handbook must include a policy addressing PHEL or, at a minimum, must reference the employer\'s obligation to provide PHEL upon the declaration of a public health emergency. Complete omission of PHEL from the handbook is non-compliant with the HFWA and fails to inform employees of this significant statutory entitlement. While PHEL is a contingent benefit (triggered only upon a public health emergency declaration), the employee handbook should describe the benefit, its triggers, the amount of leave available, and the qualifying reasons for use so that employees are informed of their rights before an emergency arises.
138	
139	**Handbook Review Note.** During the handbook review, counsel should verify that the handbook contains a PHEL policy or, at minimum, references the employer\'s obligation to provide PHEL. A handbook that addresses only accrued sick leave without mentioning PHEL is incomplete and non-compliant with the HFWA.
140	
141	**[2.3 Colorado Paid Family and Medical Leave Insurance (FAMLI)]{.underline}**
142	
143	The Colorado Paid Family and Medical Leave Insurance Act (\"FAMLI Act\"), codified at C.R.S. § 8-13.3-501 *et seq.*, establishes a statewide paid family and medical leave insurance program funded through employer and employee premium contributions. The FAMLI Act was approved by Colorado voters in November 2020 as Proposition 118. Premium collection began on January 1, 2023, and benefit payments became available beginning **January 1, 2024**. The FAMLI program is administered by the Colorado Department of Labor and Employment, Division of Family and Medical Leave Insurance (\"FAMLI Division\").
144	
145	**Benefit Entitlement.** Eligible employees may receive up to **twelve (12) weeks** of paid family and medical leave per benefit year. In cases involving pregnancy- or childbirth-related complications, the entitlement is extended to up to **sixteen (16) weeks** of paid leave per benefit year. Benefits are paid by the state FAMLI program (not directly by the employer), with weekly benefit amounts calculated based on the employee\'s average weekly wage, subject to a statutory cap.
146	
147	**Qualifying Reasons for Leave.** An employee may take FAMLI leave for any of the following qualifying reasons:
148	
149	> \(a\) A serious health condition of the employee that makes the employee unable to perform the functions of their position;
150	>
151	> \(b\) Caring for a family member with a serious health condition;
152	>
153	> \(c\) Bonding with a new child during the first twelve (12) months following the child\'s birth, adoption, or foster care placement;
154	>
155	> \(d\) A qualifying exigency related to a family member\'s active-duty military service or impending call to active duty; and
156	>
157	> \(e\) Safe leave related to domestic violence, stalking, sexual assault, or sexual abuse experienced by the employee or the employee\'s family member.
158	
159	**Eligibility Requirements.** To be eligible for FAMLI benefits, an employee must have earned at least **\$2,500 in wages** subject to FAMLI premiums during the base period (the first four of the last five completed calendar quarters prior to the claim). This eligibility threshold is significantly lower and more inclusive than federal FMLA eligibility, which requires twelve (12) months of employment and 1,250 hours worked in the preceding twelve months. As a result, many employees who would not qualify for federal FMLA leave --- including relatively new hires and part-time workers --- may be eligible for FAMLI benefits.
160	
161	**Premium Contributions.** The FAMLI program is funded through premium contributions assessed on employee wages. The total premium rate for 2025 is **0.9% of wages**, split equally between the employer (0.45%) and the employee (0.45%). Employers with fewer than ten (10) employees are not required to pay the employer\'s share of the premium but must still collect and remit the employee\'s share. Oakridge Senior Living, Inc., with **612 employees**, is well above the ten-employee threshold and is therefore required to pay both the employer and employee shares of the FAMLI premium. The employee\'s share is deducted from the employee\'s wages through payroll.
162	
163	**Interaction with Federal FMLA.** Where an employee qualifies for both FAMLI leave and federal FMLA leave, the two leaves run concurrently. However, FAMLI and FMLA differ in several important respects: FAMLI provides paid benefits (FMLA provides only unpaid, job-protected leave); FAMLI has a lower eligibility threshold; and FAMLI covers additional qualifying reasons (such as safe leave). Because of these differences, the employee handbook must address FAMLI separately from FMLA and must explain how the two programs interact when both apply. A handbook that addresses only federal FMLA without mentioning Colorado FAMLI is incomplete and does not satisfy the FAMLI Act\'s notice requirements.
164	
165	**Employer Notice Obligation.** Employers are required to provide written notice to employees about the FAMLI program. This notice must include information about how to file a FAMLI claim, the premium deductions that will be taken from the employee\'s wages, the employee\'s rights under the Act, and the job protections associated with FAMLI leave. The employer handbook is an appropriate vehicle for providing this required notice, and the handbook should include a standalone section or substantive discussion of the FAMLI program.
166	
167	**Handbook Review Note.** During the handbook review, counsel should verify that the handbook includes a standalone section or substantive discussion of Colorado FAMLI, including eligibility requirements, qualifying reasons, benefit duration, premium deductions, the claims process, job protections, and the interaction between FAMLI and FMLA. A handbook that references only federal FMLA without mentioning Colorado FAMLI is non-compliant with the FAMLI Act\'s notice requirements and fails to inform employees of a significant state-mandated benefit.
168	
169	**[2.4 Federal FMLA (Brief Cross-Reference)]{.underline}**
170	
171	The federal Family and Medical Leave Act (\"FMLA\"), 29 U.S.C. § 2601 *et seq.*, applies to employers with fifty (50) or more employees. Oakridge Senior Living, Inc., with 612 employees, is a covered employer under the FMLA. The FMLA entitles eligible employees to up to twelve (12) weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave per twelve-month period for qualifying reasons, including the employee\'s own serious health condition, caring for a family member with a serious health condition, and bonding with a new child. To be eligible for FMLA leave, an employee must have been employed for at least twelve (12) months and must have worked at least 1,250 hours during the twelve-month period immediately preceding the commencement of leave.
172	
173	This checklist focuses on Colorado-specific employment law requirements. The FMLA is referenced here for comparative purposes in connection with the Colorado FAMLI Act (see Section 2.3 above). The employee handbook should address both FMLA and FAMLI, explain the differences in eligibility and benefits between the two programs, and describe how they interact when both apply to the same leave event. Oakridge\'s handbook review should ensure that the FMLA policy is accurate and current and that the handbook does not treat FMLA as the exclusive source of family and medical leave rights, given that FAMLI now provides additional --- and in many cases, broader --- protections.
174	
175	**[Section 3: Anti-Discrimination and Harassment]{.underline}**
176	
177	This section addresses Colorado\'s anti-discrimination requirements under the Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act (\"CADA\") and related provisions. Colorado\'s anti-discrimination protections are broader than federal law in several important respects, and the employee handbook must reflect the full scope of Colorado\'s protected classes and enforcement mechanisms.
178	
179	**[3.1 Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act (CADA) --- Protected Classes]{.underline}**
180	
181	The Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act, codified at C.R.S. § 24-34-402, prohibits employment discrimination on the basis of the following protected classes:
182	
183	> • Race
184	>
185	> • Color
186	>
187	> • Religion (creed)
188	>
189	> • Sex (including pregnancy, childbirth, and related conditions)
190	>
191	> • Sexual orientation
192	>
193	> • Gender identity
194	>
195	> • Gender expression
196	>
197	> • National origin
198	>
199	> • Ancestry
200	>
201	> • Age (40 and over)
202	>
203	> • Disability (physical and mental)
204	>
205	> • Marital status
206	>
207	> • Genetic information
208	>
209	> • Veteran / Military status
210	
211	It is critical to note that Colorado\'s list of protected classes is **broader** than the protections afforded under federal Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which covers race, color, religion, sex, and national origin. Federal law provides additional protections through other statutes --- the Americans with Disabilities Act (\"ADA\") covers disability, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (\"ADEA\") covers age, and the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (\"GINA\") covers genetic information --- but even when all federal statutes are taken into account, Colorado\'s CADA provides protections that go beyond federal law. Specifically, Colorado additionally and explicitly protects: **sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, marital status, ancestry, and creed** as distinct, enumerated protected classes.
212	
213	The distinction between state and federal protected classes is not merely academic. An employer\'s Equal Employment Opportunity (\"EEO\") policy serves as a foundational statement of the employer\'s commitment to non-discrimination and compliance with applicable law. An EEO policy that lists only the federal protected classes --- race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, and age --- without also enumerating the Colorado-specific protected classes may expose the employer to several risks: it may be cited as evidence of an inadequate or incomplete non-discrimination policy in litigation; it may suggest to employees that the employer is unaware of or indifferent to state-law protections; and it may fail to satisfy the employer\'s obligation to inform employees of their full rights under Colorado law.
214	
215	**Handbook Review Note.** During the handbook review, counsel should verify that the handbook\'s EEO policy lists **all** Colorado-protected classes. At minimum, the following categories must be explicitly listed in the EEO policy: race, color, religion/creed, sex (including pregnancy), sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, national origin, ancestry, age, disability, marital status, genetic information, and veteran/military status. Omitting any of these state-protected classes from the EEO policy is a compliance deficiency that should be corrected.
216	
217	**[3.2 Enforcement Agencies and Employee Complaint Rights]{.underline}**
218	
219	Employees who believe they have been subjected to employment discrimination or harassment in violation of Colorado or federal law have the right to file an administrative charge with the applicable enforcement agency. The employee handbook should inform employees of these rights and identify the agencies to which complaints may be directed.
220	
221	**Colorado Civil Rights Division (CCRD).** The CCRD is the state enforcement agency responsible for administering and enforcing the Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act. An employee who wishes to file a state-law discrimination complaint must file a charge with the CCRD within **three hundred (300) days** of the alleged discriminatory act. Upon receipt of a charge, the CCRD investigates the allegations and may attempt to resolve the matter through mediation or conciliation. If the CCRD finds probable cause to believe that discrimination occurred, the matter may be referred for hearing before an administrative law judge or, in certain cases, to the Colorado Attorney General\'s office.
222	
223	**U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC).** The EEOC is the federal enforcement agency responsible for administering and enforcing Title VII, the ADA, the ADEA, and GINA. An employee who wishes to file a federal discrimination complaint must file a charge with the EEOC within **three hundred (300) days** of the alleged discriminatory act (the 300-day deadline applies in states, such as Colorado, that have a state enforcement agency with which the EEOC maintains a worksharing agreement).
224

1	Under the worksharing agreement between the CCRD and the EEOC, a charge filed with one agency is generally deemed to be cross-filed with the other, ensuring dual coverage. However, the employee handbook should reference **both** the CCRD and the EEOC as agencies available to employees, so that employees are fully informed of all available avenues for pursuing discrimination complaints.
2	
3	**Handbook Review Note.** During the handbook review, counsel should verify that the handbook references **both** the Colorado Civil Rights Division (CCRD) and the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) as agencies where employees may file discrimination complaints. A handbook that references only the EEOC omits the primary state enforcement agency under CADA and may not fully inform employees of their rights under Colorado law. Both agencies should be identified by name and, ideally, with contact information or a reference to how employees can locate current contact information.
4	
5	**[3.3 Harassment Prevention Requirements]{.underline}**
6	
7	Colorado law requires employers to take reasonable steps to prevent and address harassment in the workplace. While Colorado does not currently mandate a specific number of training hours by statute --- unlike California, New York, and certain other jurisdictions --- the Colorado Civil Rights Division strongly recommends that employers provide annual harassment prevention training to all employees and supervisors.
8	
9	Best practices for harassment prevention, which should be reflected in the employee handbook, include:
10	
11	> • A written anti-harassment policy that defines prohibited conduct, provides examples, and covers all forms of harassment (including sexual harassment, harassment based on any protected class, and verbal, physical, and visual harassment);
12	>
13	> • A clear reporting procedure that provides **multiple reporting channels** (e.g., direct supervisor, human resources, a designated compliance officer, and an anonymous reporting hotline), so that employees who are harassed by their supervisor have alternative avenues for reporting;
14	>
15	> • A commitment to prompt, thorough, and impartial investigation of all harassment complaints;
16	>
17	> • A clear statement of the employer\'s anti-retaliation policy, assuring employees that they will not be subjected to adverse action for reporting harassment in good faith; and
18	>
19	> • Regular training for all employees and supervisors, with additional training for managers on their obligations to report and address harassment.
20	
21	Healthcare employers such as Oakridge should be particularly attentive to the issue of patient-on-employee harassment and third-party harassment. Direct-care staff in assisted living and memory care facilities may experience verbal or physical harassment from residents, visitors, or vendors. The handbook\'s anti-harassment policy should address the employer\'s commitment to protecting employees from third-party harassment and outline the steps employees should take to report such incidents.
22	
23	**[Section 4: Restrictive Covenants (Non-Compete / Non-Solicitation)]{.underline}**
24	
25	Colorado has enacted significant restrictions on the enforceability of restrictive covenants in the employment context. The governing statute, C.R.S. § 8-2-113, was substantially amended effective August 10, 2022, and imposes strict requirements that employers must satisfy before a non-compete or non-solicitation covenant will be deemed enforceable. This section addresses the requirements applicable to non-compete agreements, customer non-solicitation agreements, and confidentiality/trade secret protections.
26	
27	**[4.1 Non-Compete Agreements]{.underline}**
28	
29	Under C.R.S. § 8-2-113, as amended effective August 10, 2022, non-compete covenants are **void and unenforceable** in Colorado as a general rule. The statute reflects Colorado\'s strong public policy in favor of employee mobility and against unreasonable restraints on an individual\'s ability to earn a livelihood. A non-compete covenant is enforceable only if it falls within one of the narrow statutory exceptions.
30	
31	**Primary Exception --- Highly Compensated Workers.** The principal exception permits enforcement of a non-compete covenant when the restricted employee earns annualized cash compensation at or above the threshold for \"highly compensated workers,\" defined as the **60th percentile of the first-quarter wages** for the state of Colorado, as published annually by the Colorado Department of Labor and Employment. For calendar year **2025**, this threshold is **\$123,750 per year**. A non-compete covenant applied to any employee earning less than \$123,750 per year in annualized cash compensation is void and unenforceable, regardless of the employee\'s role, responsibilities, or access to confidential information.
32	
33	**Notice Requirements.** Even when the compensation threshold is met, a non-compete covenant is enforceable only if the employer has provided the employee with **clear and conspicuous** written notice of the non-compete provision. The statutory notice requirements are as follows:
34	
35	> \(a\) The notice must be provided **before the worker is hired** (for new employees) or **at least fourteen (14) business days before the effective date** of the non-compete (for existing employees who are being asked to sign a new or modified non-compete);
36	>
37	> \(b\) The notice must include the **terms of the covenant**, including the activities restricted, the geographic scope (if any), and the duration of the restriction;
38	>
39	> \(c\) The notice must state that the worker has the **right to consult with an attorney** before accepting the non-compete; and
40	>
41	> \(d\) The notice must be provided as a **separate document** or, if included within a larger agreement, must be clearly and conspicuously identified.
42	
43	Failure to provide proper notice renders the non-compete void and unenforceable, regardless of whether the employee meets the compensation threshold. The notice requirements are mandatory, not merely precatory, and cannot be waived by the employee.
44	
45	**Penalties for Violation.** An employer that attempts to enforce a void non-compete covenant, or that enters into a non-compete covenant that does not comply with the statutory requirements, may be liable for actual damages suffered by the employee, injunctive relief, and reasonable attorneys\' fees. In egregious cases, a criminal penalty (Class 2 misdemeanor) may also apply. The statute contemplates both private civil enforcement by the affected employee and enforcement by the Colorado Attorney General.
46	
47	**Handbook Review Note.** If the employee handbook contains a non-compete provision or references a non-compete obligation, counsel should verify the following: (1) the non-compete applies only to employees meeting the \$123,750 per year compensation threshold; (2) the provision includes or is accompanied by the required statutory notice language; and (3) the provision states the employee\'s right to consult an attorney before accepting. A blanket non-compete applied to \"all employees\" without regard to a compensation threshold, and without the required notice provisions, is void as a matter of Colorado law and exposes the employer to damages, attorneys\' fees, and potential criminal penalties.
48	
49	**[4.2 Non-Solicitation Agreements (Customer Non-Solicitation)]{.underline}**
50	
51	Under the same statute, C.R.S. § 8-2-113, **customer non-solicitation** agreements are subject to a separate but related compensation threshold. A customer non-solicitation covenant is enforceable only for workers earning at least **sixty percent (60%) of the highly compensated worker threshold** established for non-compete agreements. For calendar year **2025**, this means that a customer non-solicitation covenant is enforceable only for employees earning at least **\$74,250 per year** (calculated as 60% × \$123,750).
52	
53	A customer non-solicitation covenant applied to an employee earning less than \$74,250 per year is void and unenforceable under Colorado law. As with non-compete covenants, the same notice requirements apply: the employer must provide clear and conspicuous written notice of the non-solicitation provision, including the terms of the covenant, the employee\'s right to consult with an attorney before accepting, and compliance with the applicable timing requirements (prior to hire for new employees; at least fourteen business days before the effective date for existing employees).
54	
55	**Employee Non-Solicitation.** It should be noted that the statute addresses **customer** non-solicitation. Non-solicitation of co-workers (i.e., employee non-solicitation or \"no-poach\" agreements) may be subject to different analysis, and the enforceability of employee non-solicitation covenants should be evaluated on a case-specific basis. This checklist addresses customer non-solicitation provisions, which are the type most commonly found in employee handbooks and employment agreements.
56	
57	**Handbook Review Note.** If the employee handbook contains a customer non-solicitation provision, counsel should verify that the provision applies only to employees earning at least \$74,250 per year and that all statutory notice requirements have been satisfied. A blanket customer non-solicitation provision applied to all employees without regard to compensation level is void as to employees below the threshold and exposes the employer to the same penalties described in Section 4.1 above.
58	
59	**[4.3 Trade Secret and Confidentiality Agreements]{.underline}**
60	
61	It is important to distinguish non-compete and non-solicitation covenants from confidentiality and trade secret protections. Colorado law, specifically C.R.S. § 8-2-113(2)(b), provides an express exception for covenants designed to protect trade secrets. Confidentiality agreements that are limited to the protection of trade secrets and genuinely confidential, proprietary information are **not** subject to the same compensation thresholds as non-compete and non-solicitation covenants. An employer may require employees at any compensation level to sign a properly drafted confidentiality or non-disclosure agreement that protects trade secrets and proprietary information.
62	
63	This distinction carries practical significance for the handbook review. If the handbook contains a single, consolidated \"restrictive covenant\" or \"post-employment obligations\" section that conflates non-compete restrictions, customer non-solicitation restrictions, and trade secret protections into a single provision, the provisions should be separated. Combining enforceable trade secret protections with potentially void non-compete or non-solicitation covenants may create ambiguity and could jeopardize the enforceability of the otherwise permissible confidentiality obligations. Best practice is to address confidentiality/trade secret obligations in a standalone section, clearly distinct from any non-compete or non-solicitation provisions.
64	
65	**[Section 5: Termination and Final Pay]{.underline}**
66	
67	This section addresses Colorado\'s requirements regarding the timing of final pay upon separation of employment and the treatment of accrued vacation or PTO at separation. Colorado imposes some of the most stringent final pay deadlines in the country, and non-compliance can result in significant penalties.
68	
69	**[5.1 Final Pay Timing Requirements]{.underline}**
70	
71	Colorado imposes strict, tiered deadlines for the payment of final wages upon an employee\'s separation from employment. The governing statute is **C.R.S. § 8-4-104**, which establishes different payment deadlines depending on the circumstances of the separation. These deadlines are mandatory and apply regardless of the employer\'s standard payroll processing schedule.
72	
73	The three-tiered structure is as follows:
74	
75	**Involuntary Termination (Employer-Initiated Discharge).** When an employer terminates an employee\'s employment --- whether for cause, without cause, as part of a reduction in force, or for any other employer-initiated reason --- all earned wages, including accrued and unused vacation or PTO, must be paid **immediately at the time of discharge**. If the employer\'s accounting unit or payroll department is not operational at the time of termination (for example, if the termination occurs after business hours or on a day when the payroll department is closed), all earned wages must be paid **no later than six (6) hours after the start of the next regular business day** on which the accounting or payroll unit is operational. This is an extremely tight deadline and requires employers to have procedures in place for expedited final paycheck processing.
76	
77	**Voluntary Resignation with at Least Three (3) Business Days\' Notice.** When an employee voluntarily resigns and provides at least three (3) business days\' advance notice of the resignation, all earned wages must be paid **on the employee\'s last day of employment**. If the employee\'s last day of employment falls on a weekend or holiday, wages must be paid on the next business day.
78	
79	**Voluntary Resignation Without at Least Three (3) Business Days\' Notice.** When an employee voluntarily resigns without providing at least three (3) business days\' notice --- for example, if the employee resigns effective immediately or provides only one or two business days\' notice --- all earned wages must be paid **within the earlier of the next regular payday or ten (10) business days** after the date of resignation.
80	
81	**Definition of \"Earned Wages.\"** For purposes of C.R.S. § 8-4-104, \"earned wages\" encompasses all compensation owed to the employee at the time of separation, including but not limited to: regular wages for all hours worked through the date of separation, overtime compensation, earned commissions, earned bonuses (to the extent the bonus has been earned and is not subject to a legitimate, prospective performance condition), and **accrued vacation or PTO** (see Section 5.2 below). The inclusion of accrued vacation/PTO in the definition of earned wages is significant and must be accounted for in the final pay calculation.
82	
83	**Penalties for Non-Compliance.** Failure to timely pay final wages subjects the employer to a statutory penalty equal to the employee\'s daily wage rate for each day that the final wages remain unpaid, up to a maximum of ten (10) days, as provided in C.R.S. § 8-4-104(3). In addition, the employee may recover the unpaid wages, the daily penalty, costs, and reasonable attorneys\' fees. For an employer the size of Oakridge, with 612 employees and regular turnover across seven facilities, the aggregate exposure from non-compliant final pay practices could be substantial.
84	
85	**Handbook Review Note.** A handbook that provides a single, blanket final-pay timeline --- such as \"your final paycheck will be issued on the next regular payday\" --- does not comply with Colorado\'s tiered final pay requirements. Such a blanket statement would violate the immediate-payment requirement for involuntary terminations and the last-day-of-employment requirement for voluntary resignations with adequate notice. The handbook must either distinguish among the three separation scenarios and state the applicable deadline for each, or, at minimum, must not contain any statement that would result in a payment deadline less favorable than the most restrictive scenario (immediate payment for involuntary termination). The recommended approach is to set forth all three scenarios with their respective deadlines so that both the Company and its employees understand the applicable requirements.
86	
87	**[5.2 Vacation/PTO Payout at Separation]{.underline}**
88	
89	Under C.R.S. § 8-4-101(14)(a)(III), accrued vacation pay is classified as \"wages\" or \"compensation\" for purposes of the Colorado Wage Claim Act. As such, accrued and unused vacation or PTO must be included in the employee\'s final paycheck upon separation from employment, regardless of the reason for separation.
90	
91	Colorado courts have generally held that earned vacation and PTO constitute compensation that must be paid at separation. Employers should ensure that their handbook policies regarding vacation or PTO payout at termination are consistent with this statutory classification. During the handbook review, counsel should examine the Company\'s PTO payout provisions to confirm that accrued PTO is treated as earned compensation that is paid upon separation. For a full analysis of whether particular PTO policy structures --- such as forfeiture-on-resignation provisions or use-it-or-lose-it policies --- are permissible under Colorado law, counsel should consult the applicable statutory text and interpretive guidance from the CDLE, as well as relevant Colorado case law addressing the scope of C.R.S. § 8-4-101(14)(a)(III).
92	
93	**[Section 6: Whistleblower and Retaliation Protections]{.underline}**
94	
95	This section addresses Colorado\'s whistleblower and anti-retaliation protections as they apply to Oakridge Senior Living, Inc. Given Oakridge\'s status as a healthcare and senior living operator, robust whistleblower protections are particularly important, as employees in these settings are frequently in a position to observe and report safety concerns, patient care issues, regulatory violations, and public health hazards.
96	
97	**[6.1 Colorado Whistleblower Protections]{.underline}**
98	
99	Multiple Colorado statutes provide protections for employees who report or oppose violations of law, safety hazards, or other protected activity in the workplace. The principal statutory authorities include:
100	
101	> • **C.R.S. § 24-114-102** --- This statute provides whistleblower protections for state employees who disclose information about actions that the employee reasonably believes are violations of law, rule, or regulation, or that constitute gross waste of public funds, or that pose a danger to public health or safety. While this statute applies most directly to state employees, it establishes a policy framework that informs whistleblower protections across all employment sectors in Colorado.
102	>
103	> • **C.R.S. § 24-34-402.5** --- This statute provides protections against retaliation for employees who raise concerns about workplace health and safety violations, including violations related to public health emergency compliance. This provision is particularly relevant in the context of healthcare employers during public health emergencies.
104	>
105	> • **C.R.S. § 8-14.4-101 \*et seq.**\* --- This statute protects employees who report, disclose, or oppose violations of Colorado\'s wage and hour laws. An employer may not retaliate against an employee for filing a wage complaint, participating in a wage investigation, or otherwise exercising rights under the Colorado Wage Claim Act.
106	
107	**Healthcare-Specific Considerations.** Employees working in healthcare and senior living facilities occupy a unique position with respect to whistleblower protections. Direct-care staff, nurses, administrators, and support personnel may observe conditions that affect patient safety, regulatory compliance, or public health, including but not limited to: inadequate staffing levels, medication errors, abuse or neglect of residents, infection control deficiencies, unsafe building conditions, and violations of licensing or certification standards. Colorado law encourages employees to report such concerns without fear of retaliation. Employees may report concerns to a range of internal and external entities, including:
108	
109	> • Internal compliance officers, safety committees, and supervisory personnel;
110	>
111	> • The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (\"CDPHE\"), which licenses and regulates assisted living and memory care facilities;
112	>
113	> • The Colorado Department of Health Care Policy and Financing;
114	>
115	> • The Colorado Department of Labor and Employment;
116	>
117	> • Local health departments; and
118	>
119	> • Law enforcement agencies, where criminal conduct is suspected.
120	
121	**Anti-Retaliation Obligation.** Employers may not discharge, discipline, threaten, demote, reduce hours, transfer to a less desirable position, or otherwise retaliate against any employee for reporting, in good faith, violations of law, safety hazards, or other protected activity. Retaliation includes not only direct adverse employment actions but also any conduct that would dissuade a reasonable employee from engaging in protected reporting activity.
122	
123	**Handbook Requirement.** An employee handbook for a healthcare employer should include a **standalone whistleblower and retaliation protection policy** that accomplishes the following objectives:
124	
125	> \(a\) Identifies the types of protected reporting activity (e.g., reporting safety concerns, regulatory violations, patient care issues, wage and hour violations, and public health hazards);
126	>
127	> \(b\) Provides **multiple reporting channels**, including both internal channels (supervisors, HR, compliance officers, anonymous hotline) and external channels (CDPHE, CDLE, EEOC, law enforcement);
128	>
129	> \(c\) Clearly and unequivocally prohibits retaliation against employees who engage in good-faith reporting;
130	>
131	> \(d\) References applicable Colorado statutes and regulatory protections;
132	>
133	> \(e\) Describes the process for investigating retaliation complaints; and
134	>
135	> \(f\) Identifies the consequences for employees or managers who engage in retaliation.
136	
137	A handbook that contains only a general \"report safety concerns\" statement embedded within a broader section --- without a dedicated whistleblower and anti-retaliation section --- is insufficient, particularly for a healthcare employer operating licensed facilities. The standalone policy serves both a compliance function (ensuring the employer meets its notice obligations) and a practical function (encouraging employees to report concerns before they escalate into regulatory violations, patient harm, or public health incidents).
138	
139	**[Section 7: Miscellaneous Colorado Employment Law Requirements]{.underline}**
140	
141	This section addresses additional Colorado employment law requirements that may be relevant to the employee handbook review but that do not fall neatly within the major topic areas addressed in Sections 1 through 6 above. While these requirements may not require extensive handbook provisions, they should be considered during the comprehensive review to ensure that the handbook is complete and consistent with Colorado law.
142	
143	**[7.1 Colorado Wage Theft Transparency Act / Wage Notice Requirements]{.underline}**
144	
145	Colorado law requires employers to provide employees with written notice of certain wage-related information at the time of hire. Pursuant to C.R.S. § 8-4-101 *et seq.* and implementing regulations, the required notice must include the employee\'s rate of pay, the pay period and designated payday, and the nature and amount of any deductions that will be taken from the employee\'s wages. This notice should be provided in writing and acknowledged by the employee. The employee handbook should include or reference the employer\'s wage notice practices and should be consistent with the information provided in the individual wage notice given to each employee at the time of hire.
146	
147	**[7.2 Posting Requirements]{.underline}**
148	
149	Colorado employers are required to display certain workplace posters and notices in a location accessible to all employees. Required postings include, but are not limited to, the COMPS Order #39 poster, the \"Notice of Paydays\" poster, the Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act poster, the FAMLI program notice, and the Healthy Families and Workplaces Act notice. While posting requirements are technically separate from handbook requirements, the employee handbook should be consistent with the information provided on required workplace posters. Inconsistencies between posted notices and handbook provisions may create confusion and compliance risk. During the handbook review, counsel should cross-reference the handbook\'s substantive provisions against current required poster content to identify any discrepancies.
150	
151	**[7.3 Personnel File Access]{.underline}**
152	
153	Under C.R.S. § 8-2-129, Colorado employees have the right to inspect their personnel file at least once per year. The employer must make the personnel file available for inspection within a reasonable period following the employee\'s request. The employee handbook should include a statement informing employees of their right to access their personnel file, the process for submitting a request, and the timeframe within which the employer will make the file available.
154	
155	**[7.4 Lawful Off-Duty Activities]{.underline}**
156	
157	C.R.S. § 24-34-402.5 prohibits employers from terminating or otherwise discriminating against employees for engaging in lawful activities outside the workplace during non-working hours, provided that such activities do not relate to a bona fide occupational requirement or do not create a conflict of interest with the employer\'s legitimate business interests. This statute is relevant to any employer policies that restrict off-duty conduct, including policies addressing social media use, outside employment or moonlighting, and other off-duty behavior. During the handbook review, any policies that impose restrictions on off-duty conduct should be evaluated for compliance with this statute. A detailed analysis of specific provisions --- such as social media policies, secondary employment policies, or codes of conduct that extend to off-duty behavior --- is beyond the scope of this statutory checklist but should be undertaken as part of the broader handbook review.
158	
159	**[7.5 At-Will Employment]{.underline}**
160	
161	Colorado recognizes the doctrine of at-will employment, under which either the employer or the employee may terminate the employment relationship at any time, with or without cause, and with or without notice, subject to applicable legal restrictions (e.g., anti-discrimination laws, retaliation protections). Best practice is to include a clear and conspicuous at-will employment disclaimer in the employee handbook, typically in the introduction or as one of the first provisions. The at-will disclaimer should be reviewed in the context of the entire handbook to ensure that no other provisions --- such as progressive discipline policies, probationary period provisions, or language suggesting that employees will be terminated only for \"just cause\" --- inadvertently create implied contractual obligations that may modify or undermine the at-will relationship. A detailed analysis of implied contract issues is beyond the scope of this statutory checklist but should be considered during the handbook review.
162

**[Appendix B: Colorado Protected Classes --- Complete List]{.underline}**

The following is a complete enumerated list of all protected classes under the Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act (CADA), C.R.S. § 24-34-402, for cross-reference during the handbook review:

> 1\. Race
>
> 2\. Color
>
> 3\. Religion / Creed
>
> 4\. Sex (including pregnancy, childbirth, and related conditions)
>
> 5\. Sexual orientation
>
> 6\. Gender identity
>
> 7\. Gender expression
>
> 8\. National origin
>
> 9\. Ancestry
>
> 10\. Age (40 and over)
>
> 11\. Disability (physical and mental)
>
> 12\. Marital status
>
> 13\. Genetic information
>
> 14\. Veteran / Military status

**Comparison with Federal Protected Classes.** Federal law provides employment discrimination protections through several statutes, including Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (covering race, color, religion, sex, and national origin), the Americans with Disabilities Act (covering disability), the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (covering age 40 and over), and the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (covering genetic information). Even when all federal statutes are considered together, Colorado\'s CADA provides additional protections that are not expressly enumerated under federal law. Specifically, Colorado adds the following protected classes beyond the core federal protections: **sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, marital status, ancestry, and creed** (as a category distinct from religion).

An EEO policy that lists only the federal protected classes will be incomplete under Colorado law. During the handbook review, the EEO policy must be compared against the complete list above to ensure that all fourteen (14) Colorado-protected classes are expressly enumerated.

**Enforcement Agencies.** Employees who believe they have been subjected to discrimination based on any of the above-listed protected classes may file a charge with the **Colorado Civil Rights Division (CCRD)** or the **U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC)**. Both agencies should be referenced in the employer\'s EEO and anti-discrimination policy, as discussed in Section 3.2 of this checklist.

Additional legal requirements --- including but not limited to occupational safety (OSHA/Colorado OSHA), workers\' compensation, immigration/I-9 compliance, and industry-specific licensing and regulatory obligations --- may apply to Oakridge\'s operations and should be addressed separately.

**OAKRIDGE SENIOR LIVING, INC.**
