Employees who violate this policy may be subject to disciplinary action, up to and including termination. All Company technology and data must be returned to the Company upon separation from employment.

**[Section 11: Progressive Discipline]{.underline}**

**[11.1 Progressive Discipline Process]{.underline}**

Oakridge Senior Living, Inc. believes in a progressive approach to discipline that is designed to give employees the opportunity to understand and correct performance or conduct deficiencies before more serious action is taken. The Company\'s progressive discipline process consists of the following four steps:

**Step 1 --- Verbal Warning.** When an employee\'s performance or conduct does not meet expectations, the supervisor will issue a verbal warning and discuss the concern with the employee. The verbal warning will be documented in the employee\'s file. During the verbal warning meeting, the supervisor will clearly describe the performance or conduct issue, explain the expected standard, and discuss what the employee can do to improve. The employee will be given the opportunity to respond and ask questions.

**Step 2 --- Written Warning.** If the employee\'s performance or conduct does not improve following a verbal warning, the supervisor will issue a formal written warning outlining the specific deficiency and the expected corrective action. The written warning will include a description of the problem, a reference to any prior verbal warning, the specific actions the employee must take to correct the deficiency, and a timeline for improvement. The employee will be asked to sign the written warning to acknowledge receipt. A signed copy will be placed in the employee\'s personnel file.

**Step 3 --- Final Written Warning.** If performance or conduct issues persist after a written warning, a final written warning will be issued. The final written warning will include a Performance Improvement Plan (PIP) with specific, measurable goals and a timeline for improvement. The PIP will outline the exact performance or behavioral standards that must be met, the support and resources available to the employee, the timeframe for achieving the stated goals, and the consequences of failing to meet the requirements of the PIP. The employee, the supervisor, and the facility director (or designee) will meet to review the PIP, and the employee will be asked to sign the final written warning and PIP.

**Step 4 --- Termination.** If the employee fails to meet the terms of the PIP or the conduct or performance issues continue, employment will be terminated. The termination decision will be reviewed and approved by the facility director and the General Counsel (or designee) prior to implementation. The employee will receive written notification of the termination and the reasons therefor.

Employees will be given the opportunity to improve performance before termination, except in cases of gross misconduct.

Oakridge reserves the right to skip any step in the progressive discipline process when, in the Company\'s sole judgment, the severity of the infraction warrants immediate action, including in cases involving gross misconduct, safety violations, or resident abuse or neglect. The Company further reserves the right to repeat any step in the process, to extend timelines for improvement, or to implement other corrective measures as the Company deems appropriate under the circumstances. The determination of whether and which step of the progressive discipline process to apply in any given situation is within the sole discretion of the Company.

Nothing in this section is intended to alter the at-will nature of employment with Oakridge Senior Living. The Company\'s use of a progressive discipline framework does not require the Company to follow the steps described above in any particular case and does not create an obligation to follow any particular sequence of disciplinary actions prior to termination.

**[11.2 Documentation]{.underline}**

All disciplinary actions, including verbal warnings, written warnings, final written warnings, PIPs, and termination notices, will be documented in writing and placed in the employee\'s personnel file maintained at the employee\'s facility. Documentation of disciplinary actions will include the date of the action, the nature of the performance or conduct issue, the specific policy or standard that was violated or not met, a summary of the discussion with the employee, and any corrective action required.

Employees have the right to submit a written response to any disciplinary action. The written response will be attached to the disciplinary documentation and placed in the employee\'s personnel file. Employees who wish to submit a written response should do so within ten (10) business days of receiving the disciplinary action. Written responses should be submitted to the supervisor who issued the disciplinary action or to the facility\'s HR representative.

Personnel files containing disciplinary documentation are maintained in a secure location at each facility and are accessible only to authorized personnel, including the employee\'s direct supervisor, the facility director, the General Counsel, and designated HR staff. Employees may request to review their own personnel file in accordance with applicable Colorado law.

**[Section 12: Restrictive Covenants]{.underline}**

**[12.1 Non-Competition Agreement]{.underline}**

As a condition of employment, all employees of Oakridge Senior Living agree that, upon separation from employment for any reason, they will not directly or indirectly engage in, own, manage, operate, consult with, or be employed by any business that competes with Oakridge Senior Living within a fifty (50) mile radius of any Oakridge facility for a period of twelve (12) months following the last day of employment.

For purposes of this section, a \"business that competes with Oakridge Senior Living\" means any entity that provides assisted living, memory care, skilled nursing, or similar senior living services to individuals within the geographic scope described above. This restriction applies regardless of whether the employee\'s role at the competing business is the same as or similar to the role the employee held at Oakridge.

The Company has invested substantial resources in the development of its care programs, operating systems, resident relationships, and proprietary business methods. The non-competition restriction is intended to protect these legitimate business interests and to prevent unfair competitive advantage gained through knowledge and experience obtained during employment with Oakridge. Employees acknowledge that the scope and duration of this restriction are reasonable and necessary in light of the Company\'s business interests and the competitive landscape in the Colorado senior living market.

This non-competition obligation is a material condition of employment and applies to all employees, regardless of position, department, or facility. Employees who were employed by Oakridge prior to the effective date of this handbook are deemed to have accepted this obligation as a condition of continued employment.

**[12.2 Non-Solicitation of Customers/Residents]{.underline}**

All employees agree that for a period of twelve (12) months following separation from employment, they will not directly or indirectly solicit, contact, or attempt to solicit any current or prospective resident or family member of a resident of any Oakridge facility for the purpose of diverting business away from Oakridge Senior Living.

This restriction applies to all forms of solicitation, whether in person, by telephone, by email, through social media, or by any other means of communication. For purposes of this section, a \"prospective resident\" means any individual or family member with whom Oakridge had meaningful contact regarding potential residency or services within the twelve (12) months preceding the employee\'s separation from employment.

The relationships between Oakridge Senior Living and its residents and their families are among the Company\'s most valuable assets. This non-solicitation restriction is intended to protect the Company\'s goodwill and the integrity of its resident relationships. Employees acknowledge that this restriction is reasonable in scope and duration and is necessary to protect the Company\'s legitimate business interests.

**[12.3 Non-Solicitation of Employees]{.underline}**

For a period of twelve (12) months following separation from employment with Oakridge Senior Living, employees agree that they will not, directly or indirectly, recruit, solicit, encourage, or induce any current employee of Oakridge Senior Living to leave employment with the Company or to accept employment with any other entity.

This restriction is intended to protect the Company\'s investment in its workforce, including the costs of recruiting, hiring, training, and retaining qualified employees in a highly competitive labor market. The restriction applies to all forms of solicitation and recruitment, whether initiated by the former employee or conducted at the direction of a new employer or other third party.

Employees acknowledge that the senior living industry faces significant workforce challenges and that the loss of trained caregivers and other staff can directly and adversely affect the quality of care provided to residents. This restriction is designed to preserve the stability and continuity of the Company\'s workforce for the benefit of residents, employees, and the Company alike.

**[12.4 Remedies for Breach]{.underline}**

In the event of a breach or threatened breach of any restrictive covenant set forth in this Section 12, Oakridge Senior Living shall be entitled to seek and obtain injunctive relief from a court of competent jurisdiction, in addition to any other remedies available at law or in equity. The employee acknowledges that a breach of any restrictive covenant would cause irreparable harm to the Company for which monetary damages alone would be an insufficient remedy.

In addition to injunctive relief, the Company may seek monetary damages, including but not limited to lost profits, diminished goodwill, and any other damages arising from the breach. The Company shall also be entitled to recover its reasonable attorney\'s fees and costs incurred in enforcing the restrictive covenants.

The restrictions set forth in this section are deemed reasonable and necessary by the Company to protect its legitimate business interests, including its confidential information, trade secrets, goodwill, customer and resident relationships, and workforce stability. If any provision of this section is found by a court of competent jurisdiction to be unreasonable or unenforceable in any respect, the court is authorized and requested to modify the provision to the minimum extent necessary to make it reasonable and enforceable, and to enforce the provision as modified.

The employee\'s obligations under this Section 12 survive the termination of the employment relationship, regardless of the reason for termination.

**[Section 13: Social Media Policy]{.underline}**

**[13.1 Purpose]{.underline}**

This Social Media Policy was added to the Employee Handbook in the March 2025 revision to address the growing use of social media by employees and its potential impact on the Company, its residents, and its staff. The proliferation of social media platforms has created new opportunities for communication and connection, but has also introduced new risks related to confidentiality, reputation, and professional conduct. This policy is intended to provide employees with clear guidelines for responsible social media use.

**[13.2 Social Media Guidelines]{.underline}**

Employees shall not post any content on social media that references Oakridge Senior Living, its residents, staff, services, or operations without prior written approval from the Communications Department.

For purposes of this policy, \"social media\" is defined broadly to include, but is not limited to, the following platforms and categories: Facebook, Instagram, X (formerly Twitter), LinkedIn, TikTok, YouTube, Snapchat, Pinterest, Reddit, personal blogs, web forums, online discussion boards, podcasts, and any other online platform or application that allows users to create, share, or exchange content, information, or opinions with others.

**Specific Prohibitions.** The following conduct is prohibited:

> • Posting, sharing, or commenting on social media content that references Oakridge Senior Living, its facilities, services, programs, residents, staff, management, or operations without prior written approval from the Communications Department
>
> • Disclosing or referencing confidential Company information, proprietary business data, trade secrets, financial information, or strategic plans on social media
>
> • Posting, sharing, or transmitting any resident information, photographs, or images on social media, including but not limited to information that could identify a resident or reveal protected health information in violation of HIPAA
>
> • Using Oakridge Senior Living\'s name, logos, trademarks, or branding on social media without prior written authorization from the Communications Department
>
> • Posting content on social media that is defamatory, threatening, harassing, or discriminatory toward the Company, its employees, residents, or families

**Consequences.** Employees who violate this Social Media Policy may be subject to disciplinary action up to and including termination of employment. The severity of the disciplinary action will depend on the nature and impact of the violation, whether confidential or resident information was involved, and any other relevant circumstances.

Employees are reminded that even when posting on personal social media accounts during non-working hours, they should exercise good judgment and discretion. Content posted online can have lasting and far-reaching consequences, both for the individual and for the Company. Employees should be mindful that their online presence may reflect upon Oakridge Senior Living, particularly when they are identifiable as employees of the Company.

Employees who have questions about whether a particular social media post or activity would be permissible under this policy should contact the Communications Department or the General Counsel before posting.

**[13.3 Personal Social Media Use]{.underline}**

Personal use of social media during working hours is discouraged and should not interfere with job performance, productivity, or the quality of resident care. Employees who wish to access personal social media accounts during the workday should do so only during authorized breaks and meal periods, and only on personal devices.

Company-owned devices, including computers, tablets, and smartphones, should not be used for personal social media activity unless the employee is on an authorized break and the activity does not interfere with business operations or consume Company bandwidth or resources. Employees should not use Company email addresses to register for or manage personal social media accounts.

Excessive personal use of social media during working hours, or personal social media use that interferes with job duties, may result in disciplinary action. Supervisors who observe that an employee\'s social media use is interfering with their work performance should address the matter through the Company\'s progressive discipline process described in Section 11 of this handbook.

**[Section 14: Dispute Resolution]{.underline}**

**[14.1 Internal Complaint Procedure]{.underline}**

Oakridge Senior Living, Inc. is committed to maintaining a positive and productive workplace. The Company encourages open communication and believes that most workplace concerns and disputes can be resolved through constructive dialogue and good-faith problem-solving.

Employees who have a work-related concern, complaint, or dispute are encouraged to first attempt to resolve the matter informally by discussing the issue with their immediate supervisor. In many cases, concerns can be addressed promptly and effectively through a direct conversation. If the concern involves the employee\'s supervisor, or if the employee is not comfortable raising the issue with their supervisor, the employee may bring the matter to the attention of the facility director.

If the matter cannot be resolved through informal discussion with the supervisor or facility director, the employee may submit a formal written complaint to the General Counsel, Denise Kowalski, at the corporate office (4501 Ponderosa Ridge Drive, Suite 200, Colorado Springs, CO 80918; telephone: (719) 555-0134; email: dkowalski@oakridgeseniorliving.com). The written complaint should include a description of the concern, the individuals involved, the dates and circumstances of the events at issue, any steps already taken to attempt to resolve the matter, and the resolution the employee is seeking.

The Company will investigate all formal written complaints promptly and will provide the employee with a written response within ten (10) business days of receipt of the complaint, or within such longer period as may be necessary to conduct a thorough investigation. The Company is committed to addressing complaints fairly and without retaliation against any employee who raises a concern in good faith.

**[14.2 Mandatory Arbitration]{.underline}**

Any and all disputes, claims, or controversies arising out of or relating to the employee\'s employment with Oakridge Senior Living, or the termination thereof, shall be resolved through final and binding arbitration. Arbitration shall be administered by a mutually agreed-upon arbitrator in Colorado Springs, Colorado, in accordance with the applicable rules of the American Arbitration Association (AAA) governing employment disputes. The arbitrator\'s decision shall be final and binding on all parties and may be entered as a judgment in any court of competent jurisdiction.

**Scope of Arbitration.** This arbitration provision covers all employment-related disputes, including but not limited to claims of wrongful termination, discrimination, harassment, retaliation, breach of contract, wage and hour violations, and any claims arising under federal, state, or local statutes, regulations, or common law. This includes, without limitation, claims under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Fair Labor Standards Act, the Family and Medical Leave Act, the Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act, the Colorado Wage Claim Act, and any other federal, state, or local law or regulation governing the employment relationship.

**Class and Collective Action Waiver.** All claims must be brought in the employee\'s individual capacity. The employee waives any right to participate in a class action, collective action, or representative proceeding of any kind. The arbitrator shall have no authority to consolidate claims, hear class or collective claims, or award relief to any person or entity other than the individual employee and the Company. This waiver applies to any and all claims, regardless of the nature of the claim or the law under which the claim arises.

**Costs and Fees.** The Company will bear the arbitrator\'s fees and all administrative costs associated with the arbitration proceeding. Each party shall bear its own attorney\'s fees and costs, unless the arbitrator determines that an award of attorney\'s fees to the prevailing party is appropriate under applicable law. The Company will not require the employee to pay any costs or fees that the employee would not have been required to pay had the claims been brought in court.

**Initiation of Arbitration.** Either party may initiate arbitration by delivering a written demand for arbitration to the other party. S=/home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/sbx.sh; R=/home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/vendor/harvey-labs/results/employment-labor/compare-employee-handbook-against-state-requirements/claude-code-session/20261016-032126; $S $R 'cat > /workspace/build/p2.py <<"EOF"
# ---------------- Title block ----------------
para("BRIARSTONE & LYLE LLP", bold=True, size=13, align=WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER, color="1F3A5F", after=0)
para("1700 Stout Street, Suite 1450 | Denver, Colorado 80202 | (303) 555-4200", size=9, align=WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER, after=10)
para("MEMORANDUM — COMPLIANCE GAP ANALYSIS", bold=True, size=15, align=WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER, color="1F3A5F", after=2)
para("Oakridge Senior Living, Inc. Employee Handbook (Revised March 14, 2025) Measured Against Colorado Employment Law", italic=True, size=11, align=WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER, after=10)

kv_table([
    ("To", "Denise Kowalski, General Counsel (Part-Time), Oakridge Senior Living, Inc.\ncc: Margaret “Meg” Tyburn, Chief Executive Officer (at Ms. Kowalski’s discretion)"),
    ("From", "Briarstone & Lyle LLP — Caitlin Reeves, Senior Associate; reviewed by Jonathan Briarstone, Lead Partner"),
    ("Date", "June 27, 2025"),
    ("Matter", "Employee Handbook Compliance Review — Matter No. 2025-OSL-0047 (engagement letter dated May 19, 2025)"),
    ("Materials reviewed", "(1) Oakridge Employee Handbook, revised March 14, 2025 (Sections 1–14 and Appendix A); (2) Oakridge Employee Census as of April 30, 2025 (Pinnacle Payroll Services; reviewed by R. Chu) — all four tabs; (3) Briarstone & Lyle Colorado Employment Law Requirements Checklist (May 2025; law current as of May 19, 2025); (4) D. Kowalski transmittal email dated June 2, 2025."),
    ("Bottom line", "The handbook is **not ready for August 1 distribution in its current form.** We identified **35 gaps**: **10 Critical, 11 High, 9 Medium and 5 Low.** Several Critical items are not merely drafting problems — they reflect pay practices that appear to be producing live wage-and-hour liability today (Denver local minimum wage, exempt salary threshold, daily overtime, rest breaks, PTO accrual and forfeiture, final pay) and a void, penalty-bearing non-compete imposed on all 612 employees. Those items require operational correction now, independent of the handbook re-issue."),
])

doc.add_heading("1. Executive Summary", level=1)
para("We compared each provision of the March 14, 2025 handbook against the firm’s Colorado requirements checklist and against current Colorado statutes, the Colorado Overtime and Minimum Pay Standards Order (COMPS Order #39, 7 CCR 1103-1) and local wage ordinances, and we tested the handbook against the April 30, 2025 census to size the affected population for each gap. The handbook is built on a 2019 multi-state template that tracks federal (FLSA/FMLA/Title VII) baselines; in nearly every area where Colorado law diverges from federal law, the handbook follows the federal rule or is silent. The most significant themes are:")
bullet("**Wage and hour (464 non-exempt employees; potentially up to 490).** The handbook states a $14.00 minimum starting wage (below the $14.81 state minimum); the census shows Denver hourly staff starting at $16.50, below Denver’s 2025 local minimum wage of $18.81; overtime omits Colorado’s 12-hour daily and 12-consecutive-hour triggers; the meal break trigger is six hours rather than five; and rest breaks are described as “encouraged but not required.” Separately, every facility pays some salaried exempt employees below Colorado’s 2025 exempt salary floor of $56,485 (at least 8 and up to 26 employees), which means they are likely misclassified under Colorado law even though they satisfy the federal $35,568 floor.")
bullet("**Paid leave (all 612 employees).** The combined PTO bank accrues at 1 hour per 40 hours worked (HFWA minimum is 1:30), imposes a 90-day use waiting period, bars temporary employees from use, lets supervisors deny leave for operational reasons, and is paired with an attendance policy that disciplines “patterns” of absence. There is no Public Health Emergency Leave (PHEL) policy, no HFWA rights notice, and **no reference at all to Colorado FAMLI** — the federal FMLA section does not satisfy Colorado’s paid family and medical leave notice obligations (answering Ms. Kowalski’s first question).")
bullet("**Separation pay (every departing employee).** The handbook pays all final wages on the next regular payday, which is unlawful for involuntary terminations (wages are due immediately), and forfeits accrued PTO on voluntary resignation, which the Colorado Supreme Court held unlawful in Nieto v. Clark’s Market, Inc., 2021 CO 48.")
bullet("**Restrictive covenants (all 612 employees).** Section 12 imposes a 50-mile, 12-month non-compete and a customer/resident non-solicit on every employee, accepted by signature on the handbook acknowledgment or “deemed accepted” by continued employment, with no statutory notice. Under C.R.S. § 8-2-113 the non-compete is void as to at least 589 employees (everyone below the 2025 $127,091 threshold) and procedurally void as to all; merely presenting it exposes Oakridge to actual damages, a $5,000 penalty per worker harmed, and attorneys’ fees (answering the third question).")
bullet("**Anti-discrimination, harassment and retaliation.** The EEO and harassment policies list only federal classes, omit seven-plus Colorado classes, still use the “severe or pervasive” hostile-environment standard that Colorado’s POWR Act abolished in 2023, identify only the EEOC (not the Colorado Civil Rights Division), and route complaints to a part-time General Counsel with no HR or hotline alternative. There is no standalone whistleblower policy — a significant gap for a licensed senior care operator — and no accommodation (pregnancy, disability, religion, lactation) policy.")
bullet("**Policies that undermine their own enforceability.** The social media policy bars any unapproved post referencing Oakridge, its staff or management (unlawful under NLRA Section 7 and in tension with C.R.S. § 24-34-402.5); the mandatory arbitration clause sits inside a handbook that disclaims contractual effect and reserves unilateral modification rights (a recognized ground for invalidity in the Tenth Circuit), lacks the federal sexual harassment/assault carve-out, and contains a confidentiality clause in conflict with Colorado’s POWR Act; and the progressive discipline section uses mandatory “will” language that erodes the at-will disclaimer (answering the at-will question raised in the transmittal).")
para("**Checklist corrections.** In completing this analysis we identified several points in our own May 2025 checklist that should be corrected before it is relied on further, most importantly the 2025 restrictive covenant thresholds ($127,091 / $76,254.60, not the 2024 figures of $123,750 / $74,250), the final pay rules (C.R.S. § 8-4-109; there is no “three business days’ notice” tier and the penalty is not a ten-day daily-wage penalty), and the rest-break count for a six-hour shift. These are set out in Section 6. The census’s restrictive-covenant eligibility columns were built on the outdated thresholds and should be recomputed.")
para("**Timing.** The August 1, 2025 distribution date is achievable for a corrected handbook if the redraft begins on receipt of this memorandum, but the restrictive covenant and arbitration provisions should be removed from the handbook and handled in separate, individually executed agreements on their own timeline. The wage-and-hour items flagged as “Act now” in Section 7 should not wait for August 1.")

doc.add_heading("2. Direct Answers to the Questions in the June 2 Transmittal", level=1)
kv_table([
    ("Q1. Does the FMLA section (Section 9) cover our Colorado paid leave obligations?", "**No.** Colorado FAMLI (C.R.S. § 8-13.3-501 et seq.; benefits payable since January 1, 2024) is a separate program with a different eligibility test ($2,500 in base-period wages vs. FMLA’s 12 months/1,250 hours), paid benefits, additional qualifying reasons (safe leave; military exigency for a broader family definition), job protection after 180 days of employment, and its own written-notice and premium-deduction obligations. The handbook needs a standalone FAMLI section explaining eligibility, the 12-week (16 with pregnancy/childbirth complications) entitlement, the 0.9% premium split (0.45% employee deduction), how to file a claim with the FAMLI Division, job protection and benefits continuation, anti-retaliation, and concurrency with FMLA and with HFWA/PTO. HFWA Public Health Emergency Leave must also be added. See Findings H-1 and H-2."),
    ("Q2. Do Colorado wage-and-hour rules diverge from the FLSA framework?", "**Yes, materially, and the handbook follows the federal framework in each instance.** Colorado requires: a $14.81 state minimum wage (and $18.81 in Denver under the Denver ordinance); overtime after 12 hours in a workday or 12 consecutive hours, not only after 40 in a week; a 30-minute duty-free meal period for shifts exceeding five hours; mandatory paid 10-minute rest breaks; an exempt salary floor of $56,485 in 2025 (vs. $35,568 federally); immediate payment of final wages on involuntary termination; and payout of all earned vacation/PTO at separation. See Findings C-1 through C-8 and M-1 through M-3. We recommend a privileged pay-practice audit using Pinnacle Payroll data (Section 8)."),
    ("Q3. Does the 2019 restrictive covenant language (Section 12) still hold up?", "**No.** The 2022 amendments to C.R.S. § 8-2-113 render the non-compete void for anyone below the highly compensated threshold ($127,091 in 2025) and the customer non-solicit void for anyone below 60% of that threshold ($76,254.60), and require a separate, signed, clear-and-conspicuous notice delivered before acceptance of an offer (new hires) or 14 days before effectiveness (current employees). On the census, all 389 hourly and all 75 salaried non-exempt employees, and at least 58 exempt employees, fall below both thresholds; at most 23 employees (3.8%) could ever be bound by a non-compete. Section 12.1–12.2 should be deleted from the handbook immediately and replaced, for the small eligible group only, with individually noticed agreements. See Finding C-9."),
    ("Q4. Do the progressive discipline section and at-will disclaimer work together?", "**Not fully.** Section 1.3 is a strong disclaimer, and Section 11.1 contains a reservation-of-rights paragraph, but Section 11.1 also states in mandatory terms that the Company “will” issue each warning in sequence and that “[e]mployees will be given the opportunity to improve performance before termination, except in cases of gross misconduct.” Under Continental Air Lines, Inc. v. Keenan, 731 P.2d 708 (Colo. 1987), that kind of promissory language can support an implied-contract or promissory estoppel claim notwithstanding a general disclaimer. The fix is drafting: convert the steps to permissive language, delete the quoted sentence, and cross-reference Section 1.3. See Finding M-6."),
])
EOF
echo ok'

input.command:
S=/home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/sbx.sh; R=/home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/vendor/harvey-labs/results/employment-labor/compare-employee-handbook-against-state-requirements/claude-code-session/20261016-032126; $S $R 'cat > /workspace/build/p3a.py <<"EOF"
F = []
def f(id, sev, title, hb, req, gap, pop, fix, act=False, lang=None):
    F.append(dict(id=id, sev=sev, title=title, hb=hb, req=req, gap=gap, pop=pop, fix=fix, act=act, lang=lang))

f("C-1", "Critical", "Stated minimum wage is below the Colorado minimum; Denver pay practice appears to violate the Denver minimum wage",
  "§ 4.2 (Minimum Starting Wage: “$14.00 per hour for all hourly positions”); § 2.3",
  "Colorado minimum wage for 2025 is $14.81/hour (C.R.S. § 8-6-109; COMPS Order #39). Since HB 19-1210 (C.R.S. § 8-6-101(3)) local governments may set higher minimums. For 2025: City and County of Denver $18.81/hour (Denver Rev. Mun. Code ch. 58, Art. VIII); City of Boulder $15.57/hour; unincorporated Boulder County $15.69/hour. All adjust each January 1.",
  "The handbook states a wage floor $0.81 below the state minimum — non-compliant on its face (Checklist § 1.1). More seriously, the census shows the lowest hourly rate at the Denver facility is $16.50, which is $2.31/hour below Denver’s 2025 minimum. The bottom of the Denver salaried non-exempt band ($39,000/yr ≈ $18.75/hour at 40 hours) is also below $18.81. Neither the handbook nor the checklist addresses local minimum wages.",
  "Statement: all 389 hourly employees. Pay practice: up to 76 Denver hourly employees plus any Denver salaried non-exempt employees (19 in band) paid below $18.81/hour. Boulder hourly rates ($16.50 minimum) clear the Boulder city and county minimums, subject to confirming the facility’s jurisdiction.",
  ["Replace § 4.2 with a jurisdiction-neutral floor (model language below); never hard-code a dollar figure.",
   "Act now: have Pinnacle pull every Denver employee whose effective hourly rate fell below $18.81 at any point since January 1, 2025; adjust rates prospectively and pay back wages (plus any shift where overtime was computed on the lower rate). Confirm the Denver facility address is within the City and County of Denver and that the Boulder facility is within the City of Boulder or unincorporated county.",
   "Calendar an annual December review of state and local minimums (Denver and the state each publish the next year’s rate in the fall)."],
  act=True,
  lang="“Oakridge pays every employee at least the minimum wage required for the location where the work is performed — the Colorado minimum wage or, where higher, the applicable local minimum wage (for example, in the City and County of Denver or the City of Boulder). Minimum wage rates change each January 1, and current rates are posted at every facility.”")

f("C-2", "Critical", "Salaried exempt employees paid below Colorado’s exempt salary threshold; handbook keys exemption to the FLSA",
  "§ 2.2 (Exempt and Non-Exempt Classifications); census “Compensation by Classification” and “Salary Band Summary” tabs",
  "COMPS Order #39, Rule 2.5 requires executive, administrative and professional employees to be paid a salary of at least $56,485 in 2025 (the federal FLSA floor is $684/week = $35,568 following the November 15, 2024 vacatur of the 2024 DOL rule in Texas v. U.S. Dep’t of Labor). Colorado’s duties tests (COMPS Rule 2.2) must also be met. A misclassified employee is owed Colorado overtime (weekly and daily), meal/rest compliance, and penalties; limitations period is two years, three if willful (C.R.S. § 8-4-122).",
  "§ 2.2 describes exemption “in accordance with the Fair Labor Standards Act” and says exempt employees are exempt from “the FLSA.” The census shows the minimum exempt salary at every facility is below $56,485 (Colorado Springs $52,000; Denver $54,000; Boulder $51,500; Fort Collins $50,000; Pueblo $48,500; Grand Junction $49,000; Durango $48,000). The checklist does not address the Colorado salary threshold.",
  "At least 8 salaried exempt employees (the $45,000–$54,999 band) are below the threshold, and up to 18 more in the $55,000–$64,999 band may be — i.e., 8 to 26 employees (5%–18% of the 148 exempt group). Every facility is affected; the acquired facilities have the lowest floors.",
  ["Act now: obtain an employee-level list (title, duties, salary) of all exempt employees below $56,485. For each, either raise salary to at least $56,485 (and confirm the Colorado duties test is met) or reclassify as non-exempt prospectively.",
   "Quantify back overtime under counsel’s direction for the two-year (three if willful) look-back; consider a structured remediation payment.",
   "Revise § 2.2 to reference both FLSA and Colorado COMPS Order duties and salary tests and to note that the Colorado threshold is adjusted annually. Remove the statement that RNs in “supervisory roles” are exempt unless their duties and salary qualify."],
  act=True)

f("C-3", "Critical", "Overtime policy omits Colorado’s daily (12-hour) and 12-consecutive-hour triggers",
  "§ 4.3 (Overtime Pay: overtime only for hours “in excess of forty (40) hours in a single workweek”)",
  "COMPS Order #39, Rule 4.1.1: overtime at 1.5× the regular rate for hours worked over (a) 40 per workweek, (b) 12 per workday, or (c) 12 consecutive hours regardless of when the workday starts. The regular rate must include shift differentials and non-discretionary bonuses (COMPS Rule 1.8).",
  "Only the federal weekly trigger is stated (Checklist § 1.2). For a 24/7 care operator using 12-hour CNA/LPN/RN shifts, any shift overrun (handover, resident emergencies, mandatory holdover) beyond 12 hours triggers daily overtime even in a sub-40-hour week. The handbook’s reference to LPN “shift differential” (§ 4.2) also flags a regular-rate issue.",
  "All 464 non-exempt employees (389 hourly; 75 salaried non-exempt), plus any exempt employees reclassified under C-2.",
  ["Replace § 4.3’s trigger sentence with the model language below and add a regular-rate sentence.",
   "Act now: confirm with Pinnacle that daily (>12) and consecutive-hour (>12) overtime is being calculated; run a look-back of shifts over 12 hours for at least the past two years and pay any shortfall.",
   "Keep the prior-authorization rule but state expressly that all overtime worked will be paid."],
  act=True,
  lang="“Non-exempt employees are paid one and one-half times their regular rate of pay for all hours worked (1) over 40 in a workweek, (2) over 12 in a workday, or (3) over 12 consecutive hours, regardless of whether those hours span two workdays. Hours are not double-counted. The regular rate includes shift differentials and non-discretionary bonuses.”")

f("C-4", "Critical", "Meal period triggered at six hours instead of five",
  "§ 4.4 (Meal Breaks: “shifts of more than six (6) hours”)",
  "COMPS Order #39, Rule 5.1: an uninterrupted, duty-free meal period of at least 30 minutes is required when a shift exceeds five consecutive hours; where the nature of the work makes an uninterrupted meal period impractical, the employee must be permitted an on-duty meal period that is fully paid. To the extent practical, the meal period should be scheduled at least one hour after the shift starts and one hour before it ends.",

  ["Replace the rest-break paragraph with the model language below.",

  lang="“Non-exempt employees are entitled to a paid, uninterrupted 10-minute rest break for every four hours worked or major fraction of four hours (for example, one break for a shift of more than 2 and up to 6 hours, two breaks for more than 6 and up to 10 hours, and three breaks for more than 10 and up to 14 hours). f("C-7", "Critical", "PTO use restrictions conflict with HFWA (waiting period, temporary-employee bar, operational denials, documentation, increments)",

  "The 90-day waiting period and the temporary-employee bar each deny HFWA leave outright.   "All new hires in their first 90 days, all temporary employees, all part-time employees (bereavement), and any employee whose PTO request has an HFWA purpose.",
  ["Add an “HFWA-protected leave” subsection: the first 48 hours of PTO used in a benefit year for an HFWA purpose are available as accrued from day one, may not be denied for operational reasons, and are subject only to HFWA notice and documentation rules.",
   "Delete the introductory-period and temporary-employee use bars and the “PTO usage history” factor; limit documentation to absences of four or more consecutive workdays.",
   "Amend § 7.2 to allow part-time employees (and all employees for non-immediate family) to use HFWA-eligible PTO for bereavement."],

f("C-8", "Critical", "Final pay paid on the next regular payday for all separations, including involuntary terminations",
  "§ 4.7 (Final Pay: “whether voluntary or involuntary … issued on the next regular payday”)",
  "C.R.S. § 8-4-109(1)(a): when the employer terminates the employment, all earned wages are due immediately; if the employer’s accounting unit is not regularly scheduled to be operational, no later than six hours after the start of its next regular workday (24 hours if the accounting unit is off-site). § 8-4-109(1)(b): when the employee quits, wages are due on the next regular payday.   "The handbook’s single “next regular payday” rule is lawful for resignations but unlawful for every involuntary termination. The property-return deduction sentence must not delay final pay. Note: our May checklist (§ 5.1) states a three-tier rule (including a “three business days’ notice” tier) and a ten-day daily-wage penalty; those points are incorrect and are corrected in Section 6.",
  "Every involuntary separation across all seven facilities. Each late final check after a written demand carries a minimum $1,000 penalty.",
  ["Replace § 4.7 with the model language below.",
   "Act now: implement an off-cycle final-pay protocol with Pinnacle (manual check or same-day direct deposit; accrued PTO included) and train facility directors not to conduct terminations without the final check prepared.",
   "Have the property-return clause reference only deductions permitted by C.R.S. § 8-4-105 and confirm in writing that such deductions never delay final pay."],
  act=True,
  lang="“If Oakridge ends your employment, all wages you have earned — including accrued, unused PTO — will be paid at the time of separation, or, if payroll is not operating at that time, within the time required by Colorado law (no later than six hours after the start of payroll’s next regular workday, or 24 hours if payroll is processed off-site). f("C-9", "Critical", "Blanket non-compete and customer non-solicit imposed on all employees without statutory notice",
  "§ 12.1 (12-month, 50-mile non-compete for “all employees, regardless of position”; current employees “deemed to have accepted”); § 12.2 (12-month resident/family non-solicit); Appendix A acknowledgment (“agree to … the restrictive covenant provisions”)",
  "C.R.S. § 8-2-113 (as amended eff. Aug. 10, 2022): non-competes are void unless the worker earns at least the highly compensated threshold — **$127,091 for 2025** — and the covenant is for the protection of trade secrets and no broader than reasonably necessary; customer non-solicits require at least 60% of that threshold — **$76,254.60 for 2025** (§ 8-2-113(2)(b), (2)(d)). Notice must be provided in a separate document, in clear and conspicuous terms, signed by the worker, before acceptance of an offer (prospective workers) or at least 14 days before the covenant takes effect or before a change in conditions providing consideration (current workers) (§ 8-2-113(4)). An employer that enters into, presents as a term of employment, or attempts to enforce a void covenant is liable for actual damages, a penalty of $5,000 per worker or prospective worker harmed, and attorneys’ fees (§ 8-2-113(8)). Separately, 2025 legislation (SB 25-083, effective August 6, 2025) further restricts covenants for certain health-care providers; confirm application to any physicians or advanced practice nurses on staff.",
  "Section 12.1–12.2 is a 2019 template provision that predates the 2022 amendments and is void as applied to nearly the entire workforce. It is also procedurally void as to everyone: there is no separate notice, the “deemed acceptance” mechanism for existing employees is inconsistent with the 14-day signed-notice rule, and bundling covenant assent into a handbook acknowledgment is not “separate.” A 50-mile radius around any of seven facilities covers most of Colorado’s population and would be overbroad even for eligible executives. Re-issuing the handbook with § 12 intact on August 1 would itself be a fresh “presentation” to all 612 employees.",
  "Using the 2025 thresholds: non-compete eligible at most 23 employees (the census counts 23 at ≥$123,750; an unknown number of the 12 in the $123,750–$149,999 band are below $127,091), so at least 589 employees (96%) cannot be bound. Customer non-solicit eligible: 65 employees confirmed above $90,000, plus some of the 25 in the $74,250–$89,999 band — at most 90; at least 522 employees (85%), including every hourly and salaried non-exempt employee, cannot be bound. Theoretical penalty ceiling for presentation to all 612: about $3.06 million plus damages and fees.",
  ["Delete §§ 12.1 and 12.2 from the handbook and remove covenant assent from the Appendix A acknowledgment.",
   "Act now: stop presenting the covenant to new hires; send all current employees a short written notice that Oakridge will not enforce the non-compete or customer non-solicit in the prior handbook (or any predecessor Peak Vista/Western Slope covenant) against them. This narrows exposure and supports a good-faith defense.",
   "For the eligible group only (verify each person’s annualized cash compensation against $127,091 / $76,254.60), use standalone agreements with the statutory notice, a signature line, the 14-day timing, a reasonable scope tied to trade secrets, and Colorado choice of law and forum (§ 8-2-113(6)).",
   "Move confidentiality and trade-secret protection to a separate section (see the § 10.4 discussion), limited to genuine trade secrets and confidential information and including the Defend Trade Secrets Act immunity notice (18 U.S.C. § 1833(b))."],
  act=True)

f("C-10", "Critical", "Accrued PTO forfeited on voluntary resignation",
  "§ 5.4 (PTO Payout at Separation: “Unused PTO is forfeited upon voluntary resignation”)",
  "Earned vacation pay is “wages” (C.R.S. § 8-4-101(14)(a)(III)) and must be paid at separation; the Colorado Supreme Court held that an employer may not forfeit earned vacation, regardless of the reason for separation (Nieto v. Clark’s Market, Inc., 2021 CO 48). Agreements purporting to waive wage rights are void (C.R.S. § 8-4-125). CDLE guidance treats a combined PTO bank that may be used for vacation as vacation pay payable at separation.",
  "The forfeiture clause is unlawful, and the handbook encourages employees to “use their accrued PTO prior to submitting a resignation,” confirming the practice.   "Every voluntary resignation (likely the majority of separations in a high-turnover care workforce) across all seven facilities, plus acquired-facility employees under any predecessor forfeiture policy.",
  ["Replace § 5.4 with: “Accrued, unused PTO is paid at your final rate of pay upon any separation from employment, voluntary or involuntary.”",
   "Act now: suspend forfeitures immediately; have Pinnacle identify voluntary resignations within the limitations period (two years, three if willful; C.R.S. § 8-4-122) where PTO was forfeited, and pay the balances (we recommend counsel-directed remediation with a release-free payment and cover letter).",
   "Accrual caps (§ 5.3) may remain — a cap prevents further accrual and is not a forfeiture."],
  act=True)

  lang="“If Oakridge ends your employment, all wages you have earned — including accrued, unused PTO — will be paid at the time of separation, or, if payroll is not operating at that time, within the time required by Colorado law (no later than six hours after the start of payroll’s next regular workday, or 24 hours if payroll is processed off-site). If you resign, your final wages, including accrued, unused PTO, will be paid on the next regular payday.”")

f("C-9", "Critical", "Blanket non-compete and customer non-solicit imposed on all employees without statutory notice",
  "§ 12.1 (12-month, 50-mile non-compete for “all employees, regardless of position”; current employees “deemed to have accepted”); § 12.2 (12-month resident/family non-solicit); Appendix A acknowledgment (“agree to … the restrictive covenant provisions”)",
  "C.R.S. § 8-2-113 (as amended eff. Aug. 10, 2022): non-competes are void unless the worker earns at least the highly compensated threshold — **$127,091 for 2025** — and the covenant is for the protection of trade secrets and no broader than reasonably necessary; customer non-solicits require at least 60% of that threshold — **$76,254.60 for 2025** (§ 8-2-113(2)(b), (2)(d)). Notice must be provided in a separate document, in clear and conspicuous terms, signed by the worker, before acceptance of an offer (prospective workers) or at least 14 days before the covenant takes effect or before a change in conditions providing consideration (current workers) (§ 8-2-113(4)). An employer that enters into, presents as a term of employment, or attempts to enforce a void covenant is liable for actual damages, a penalty of $5,000 per worker or prospective worker harmed, and attorneys’ fees (§ 8-2-113(8)). Separately, 2025 legislation (SB 25-083, effective August 6, 2025) further restricts covenants for certain health-care providers; confirm application to any physicians or advanced practice nurses on staff.",
  "Section 12.1–12.2 is a 2019 template provision that predates the 2022 amendments and is void as applied to nearly the entire workforce. It is also procedurally void as to everyone: there is no separate notice, the “deemed acceptance” mechanism for existing employees is inconsistent with the 14-day signed-notice rule, and bundling covenant assent into a handbook acknowledgment is not “separate.” A 50-mile radius around any of seven facilities covers most of Colorado’s population and would be overbroad even for eligible executives. Re-issuing the handbook with § 12 intact on August 1 would itself be a fresh “presentation” to all 612 employees.",
  "Using the 2025 thresholds: non-compete eligible at most 23 employees (the census counts 23 at ≥$123,750; an unknown number of the 12 in the $123,750–$149,999 band are below $127,091), so at least 589 employees (96%) cannot be bound. Customer non-solicit eligible: 65 employees confirmed above $90,000, plus some of the 25 in the $74,250–$89,999 band — at most 90; at least 522 employees (85%), including every hourly and salaried non-exempt employee, cannot be bound. Theoretical penalty ceiling for presentation to all 612: about $3.06 million plus damages and fees.",
  ["Delete §§ 12.1 and 12.2 from the handbook and remove covenant assent from the Appendix A acknowledgment.",
   "Act now: stop presenting the covenant to new hires; send all current employees a short written notice that Oakridge will not enforce the non-compete or customer non-solicit in the prior handbook (or any predecessor Peak Vista/Western Slope covenant) against them. This narrows exposure and supports a good-faith defense.",
   "For the eligible group only (verify each person’s annualized cash compensation against $127,091 / $76,254.60), use standalone agreements with the statutory notice, a signature line, the 14-day timing, a reasonable scope tied to trade secrets, and Colorado choice of law and forum (§ 8-2-113(6)).",
   "Move confidentiality and trade-secret protection to a separate section (see the § 10.4 discussion), limited to genuine trade secrets and confidential information and including the Defend Trade Secrets Act immunity notice (18 U.S.C. § 1833(b))."],
  act=True)

f("C-10", "Critical", "Accrued PTO forfeited on voluntary resignation",
  "§ 5.4 (PTO Payout at Separation: “Unused PTO is forfeited upon voluntary resignation”)",
  "Earned vacation pay is “wages” (C.R.S. § 8-4-101(14)(a)(III)) and must be paid at separation; the Colorado Supreme Court held that an employer may not forfeit earned vacation, regardless of the reason for separation (Nieto v. Clark’s Market, Inc., 2021 CO 48). Agreements purporting to waive wage rights are void (C.R.S. § 8-4-125). CDLE guidance treats a combined PTO bank that may be used for vacation as vacation pay payable at separation.",
  "The forfeiture clause is unlawful, and the handbook encourages employees to “use their accrued PTO prior to submitting a resignation,” confirming the practice. Every voluntary resignation since at least 2021 is a potential wage claim with § 8-4-109 penalties. The checklist (§ 5.2) left this question open; the law is settled.",
  "Every voluntary resignation (likely the majority of separations in a high-turnover care workforce) across all seven facilities, plus acquired-facility employees under any predecessor forfeiture policy.",
  ["Replace § 5.4 with: “Accrued, unused PTO is paid at your final rate of pay upon any separation from employment, voluntary or involuntary.”",
   "Act now: suspend forfeitures immediately; have Pinnacle identify voluntary resignations within the limitations period (two years, three if willful; C.R.S. § 8-4-122) where PTO was forfeited, and pay the balances (we recommend counsel-directed remediation with a release-free payment and cover letter).",
   "Accrual caps (§ 5.3) may remain — a cap prevents further accrual and is not a forfeiture."],
  act=True)
EOF
echo ok'

S=/home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/sbx.sh; R=/home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/vendor/harvey-labs/results/employment-labor/compare-employee-handbook-against-state-requirements/claude-code-session/20261016-032126; $S $R 'cat > /workspace/build/p3b.py <<"EOF"
f("H-1", "High", "No Colorado FAMLI policy or notice; FMLA treated as the exclusive family/medical leave program",
  "§ 9 (FMLA only); § 4.6 (required deductions list omits the FAMLI premium); § 7 (no FAMLI cross-reference)",
  "Paid Family and Medical Leave Insurance Act, C.R.S. § 8-13.3-501 et seq. (benefits since Jan. 1, 2024): up to 12 weeks of paid leave per benefit year (16 with pregnancy/childbirth complications); eligibility on $2,500 of base-period wages; qualifying reasons include own or family member’s serious health condition, bonding, military exigency, and safe leave; job protection and health-benefit continuation for employees employed at least 180 days (C.R.S. § 8-13.3-509); anti-retaliation; written notice of rights, claims process and premium deductions; 2025 premium 0.9% of wages, split 0.45%/0.45% for employers of 10+ (Checklist § 2.3). Up to 12 additional weeks for neonatal intensive care stays begin in 2026 (SB 24-235).",
  "The handbook never mentions FAMLI. This answers Ms. Kowalski’s first question: FMLA language does not satisfy FAMLI. Because FAMLI eligibility is far broader than FMLA’s 12-month/1,250-hour test, a large share of the workforce (including recent hires at the acquired facilities and part-time staff) has FAMLI rights but no FMLA rights.",
  "All 612 employees. Premium deduction applies to all wages; job protection applies after 180 days.",
  ["Add a standalone “Colorado Paid Family and Medical Leave (FAMLI)” section covering eligibility, reasons, duration, how to apply to the FAMLI Division, notice to Oakridge, premium deductions, job protection and benefits continuation, intermittent leave, and anti-retaliation.",
   "Add a concurrency paragraph: FAMLI runs concurrently with FMLA where both apply; employees may (but cannot be required to) use PTO to supplement FAMLI benefits; HFWA-protected leave cannot be required to be exhausted first.",
   "Add the FAMLI employee premium to § 4.6 and include the FAMLI notice in a handbook appendix. Refer to “the current premium rate” rather than hard-coding 0.9%; the rate is reset annually."],
  act=False)

f("H-2", "High", "No HFWA Public Health Emergency Leave (PHEL) policy",
  "§ 5 (PTO) and § 7 (Leaves) — no PHEL reference",
  "C.R.S. § 8-13.3-405: upon a federal, state or local public health emergency declaration, employers must provide supplemental paid leave — 80 hours for employees who normally work 40 or more hours per week; for others, the greater of their scheduled hours or actual hours worked in a 14-day period — in addition to accrued sick leave, available through four weeks after the emergency ends, for isolation, diagnosis/care, caring for a family member, school/childcare closures, and heightened-risk conditions (Checklist § 2.2).",
  "PHEL is completely omitted. For a senior care operator — the population most exposed during a respiratory-disease emergency — this is both a compliance gap and an operational planning gap.",
  "All 612 employees (contingent benefit).",
  ["Add a PHEL subsection describing the trigger, amount, uses, relationship to PTO (separate and additional; no exhaustion requirement), and documentation limits.",
   "Coordinate with infection-control and staffing policies so PHEL use is not penalized under the attendance policy."])

f("H-3", "High", "Missing HFWA rights notice and other required HFWA content",
  "§ 5 generally; § 7.2; Appendix (no notices)",
  "C.R.S. § 8-13.3-408 requires employers to notify employees of their HFWA rights (including in the employee handbook where one exists) and to post the HFWA notice. HFWA also requires: broad “family member” coverage; confidentiality of health and domestic-violence information; no requirement that the employee find a replacement worker; reinstatement of accrued sick leave on rehire within six months; and that employees of a predecessor employer retain accrued sick leave when a successor takes over (C.R.S. § 8-13.3-403).",
  "The handbook contains none of the required HFWA disclosures. The successor rule is directly relevant to the 2024 acquisitions (see H-11).",
  "All 612 employees.",
  ["Add an HFWA notice paragraph (the CDLE template language may be adapted) and include the HFWA poster text in a notices appendix.",
   "Add rehire-reinstatement and confidentiality language; define “family member” consistently with HFWA."])

f("H-4", "High", "Attendance and PTO-scheduling rules penalize protected leave",
  "§ 10.3 (absence call-in “in no event later than two (2) hours before” the shift; discipline for “patterns” such as Monday/Friday absences, “even when reported”); § 5.2 (supervisors weigh “PTO usage history”); § 7.4 (job abandonment)",
  "HFWA (C.R.S. § 8-13.3-407) prohibits counting protected sick leave as an absence that may lead to discipline; FAMLI (C.R.S. § 8-13.3-509) and FMLA (29 C.F.R. § 825.220(c)) bar using protected leave as a negative factor; for unforeseeable HFWA leave the employee need only give notice as soon as practicable.",
  "As written, an employee who calls in sick 90 minutes before a shift, or whose sick days fall on Mondays, can be disciplined. The language “taking into account … any applicable legal protections” is too vague to cure the problem.",
  "All 612 employees; supervisors at all seven facilities apply the policy.",
  ["Add an express carve-out: absences protected by HFWA, PHEL, FAMLI, FMLA, ADA/CADA accommodation, workers’ compensation, jury, voting, military or domestic-violence leave are not counted as occurrences and are not considered in discipline or PTO scheduling.",
   "Change the call-in rule to “as soon as practicable, and where possible at least two hours before your shift.”",
   "Delete “PTO usage history” as a scheduling factor."])

f("H-5", "High", "EEO and harassment policies omit Colorado-protected classes",
  "§ 3.1 and § 3.2 (list only race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age, disability and veteran status)",
  "Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act, C.R.S. § 24-34-402, also protects creed, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, ancestry, marital status, genetic information, pregnancy/childbirth and related conditions (§ 24-34-402.3), and — through the CROWN Act (HB 20-1048) — hair texture, hair type and protective hairstyles as part of race; military status is protected under C.R.S. § 28-3-506; lawful off-duty conduct under § 24-34-402.5 (Checklist § 3.1, App. B).",
  "At least seven Colorado classes are missing (creed, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, ancestry, marital status, genetic information), pregnancy is not called out, and hairstyle is absent from both the handbook and our checklist. Genetic information is also federally protected (GINA).",
  "All 612 employees and all applicants.",
  ["Replace the class list in §§ 3.1 and 3.2 with the model language below."],
  lang="“Oakridge prohibits discrimination and harassment based on race (including hair texture, hair type and protective hairstyles), color, religion, creed, sex, pregnancy, childbirth and related conditions, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, national origin, ancestry, age (40 and over), physical or mental disability, marital status, genetic information, veteran or military status, lawful off-duty conduct as protected by Colorado law, or any other status protected by federal, state or local law.”")

f("H-6", "High", "Harassment definition uses the abolished “severe or pervasive” standard; complaint channels are thin",
  "§ 3.2 (hostile environment requires conduct “so severe or pervasive”); § 3.3 (report to supervisor, facility director, or the part-time General Counsel only)",
  "Protecting Opportunities and Workers’ Rights (POWR) Act, SB 23-172 (eff. Aug. 7, 2023): harassment under CADA need not be severe or pervasive (C.R.S. § 24-34-402(1.3)); an employer’s affirmative defense depends on maintaining a program reasonably designed to prevent harassment, deter harassers and protect employees, including a distributed policy, a complaint process with multiple avenues, training, and prompt, reasonable remedial action (C.R.S. § 24-34-402(1.5)). Checklist § 3.3 recommends multiple channels including a hotline.",
  "The “severe or pervasive” language misstates Colorado law and invites employees (and supervisors) to under-report. The only escalation path above a facility director is a part-time General Counsel available in the office Tuesday through Thursday; there is no HR function, no hotline, and no alternative when the facility director is the subject. The General Counsel’s phone number in §§ 3.3 and 14.1 ((719) 555-0134) differs from Ms. Kowalski’s signature block ((719) 555-0148).",
  "All 612 employees; heightened for direct-care staff exposed to resident and family-member conduct.",
  ["Redefine harassment per the POWR Act (unwelcome conduct directed at an employee because of a protected characteristic that is subjectively offensive and objectively offensive to a reasonable person in the same protected class), deleting “severe or pervasive.”",
   "Add at least two additional channels: a corporate HR designee and a 24/7 anonymous hotline or web portal; allow reports to any manager; state that employees need not report to anyone involved in the conduct.",
   "Add a resident-behavior protocol (dementia-related conduct) alongside the existing third-party harassment paragraph, and document annual training for all staff and supervisors."])

f("H-7", "High", "No standalone whistleblower and anti-retaliation policy for a licensed health-care operator",
  "§ 6.2 (safety concerns to supervisor, director or Safety Committee only); § 3.3 and § 6.3 (non-retaliation limited to discrimination and workers’ compensation); § 10.2 (failure to report abuse is misconduct)",
  "Relevant protections include: C.R.S. § 8-2-123 (health-care workers reporting patient-safety information); C.R.S. § 8-14.4-101 et seq. (Public Health Emergency Whistleblower law); C.R.S. § 8-4-120 (wage complaints); C.R.S. §§ 8-13.3-407 and -509 (HFWA and FAMLI); C.R.S. § 24-34-402(1)(e) (CADA); OSHA § 11(c); the federal False Claims Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3730(h), and Colorado’s Medicaid False Claims Act; and mandatory elder-abuse reporting under C.R.S. § 18-6.5-108. Checklist § 6.1 requires a standalone policy with internal and external channels (CDPHE, HCPF, CDLE, EEOC/CCRD, law enforcement).",
  "The handbook has only a general “report safety concerns” statement — exactly the configuration the checklist identifies as insufficient. Several of the checklist’s statutory citations for this section are inaccurate and should not be copied into the handbook (see Section 6).",
  "All 612 employees; particularly the 389 hourly direct-care staff.",
  ["Add a standalone “Reporting Concerns and Non-Retaliation” section covering protected activities (patient/resident safety, abuse/neglect, infection control, staffing, licensing, billing/Medicaid, wage-hour, discrimination, public-health), internal channels including a hotline, external agencies (CDPHE, HCPF, CDLE, CCRD, EEOC, OSHA, law enforcement, the long-term care ombudsman), investigation steps, and discipline for retaliators.",
   "State that nothing in the handbook (including confidentiality and social media rules) restricts reports to government agencies."])

f("H-8", "High", "No accommodation policies (disability, pregnancy, religion, lactation)",
  "No provision; § 6.3 and § 6.4 mention accommodations only in passing",
  "CADA and ADA (disability accommodation and interactive process); C.R.S. § 24-34-402.3 (pregnancy, childbirth and related-condition accommodations, with a written notice-of-rights obligation to new and existing employees); federal Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (eff. June 27, 2023); religious accommodation under Title VII and CADA (Groff v. DeJoy, 600 U.S. 447 (2023), “substantial increased costs” standard); Workplace Accommodations for Nursing Mothers Act, C.R.S. § 8-13.5-101 et seq. (reasonable break time and a private, non-restroom space for up to two years after birth) and the federal PUMP Act.",
  "The handbook has no accommodation request process or pregnancy notice. For a physically demanding, predominantly female caregiving workforce, pregnancy and lifting-restriction accommodations are a frequent source of claims.",
  "All 612 employees.",
  ["Add a consolidated “Reasonable Accommodations” section with an interactive-process description and a single request channel, plus a lactation subsection.",
   "Include the C.R.S. § 24-34-402.3 pregnancy-rights notice in the notices appendix and distribute it with the August 1 handbook."])

f("H-9", "High", "Social media policy bars protected employee speech",
  "§ 13.2 (no post referencing Oakridge, “its residents, staff, services, or operations” or “management” without prior written approval; bar on content “defamatory … toward the Company”); § 13.3",
  "NLRA § 7 protects non-supervisory employees’ concerted discussion of wages, staffing, safety and working conditions, including online, whether or not unionized; overbroad rules are evaluated under Stericycle, Inc., 372 NLRB No. 113 (2023). C.R.S. § 24-34-402.5 limits discipline for lawful off-duty conduct; C.R.S. § 8-2-127 bars requiring access to personal social media accounts; Colorado law protects wage discussions (C.R.S. § 8-5-102).",
  "A prior-approval requirement for any post mentioning co-workers or management would chill core protected activity (for example, CNAs posting about short staffing) and could not lawfully be enforced. The “Communications Department” referenced as the approval body may not exist at Oakridge.",
  "All non-supervisory employees (the large majority of 612).",
  ["Narrow § 13.2 to: (i) resident privacy/PHI and resident images; (ii) genuinely confidential business information and trade secrets; (iii) harassment, threats and discrimination; (iv) speaking on behalf of the Company without authorization; and (v) use of logos to imply endorsement.",
   "Add a savings clause: “Nothing in this policy restricts employees’ rights to discuss wages, hours, staffing or other terms and conditions of employment, to engage in protected concerted activity, or to report concerns to government agencies.”",
   "Confirm who approves official Company posts, and add the § 8-2-127 assurance that Oakridge will not request personal account credentials."])

f("H-10", "High", "Mandatory arbitration clause is likely unenforceable as drafted and conflicts with federal and Colorado law",
  "§ 14.2 (mandatory arbitration, class waiver, confidentiality); § 14.3 (delegation); Appendix A (assent by signing handbook acknowledgment); §§ 1.2 and Appendix A (handbook “not a contract”; Company may modify “at any time … with or without notice”)",
  "An arbitration promise in a handbook that disclaims contractual intent and reserves unilateral modification is illusory (Dumais v. American Golf Corp., 299 F.3d 1216 (10th Cir. 2002)). The Ending Forced Arbitration of Sexual Assault and Sexual Harassment Act, 9 U.S.C. §§ 401–402, lets an employee void pre-dispute arbitration of sexual-harassment and sexual-assault disputes. The POWR Act (C.R.S. § 24-34-407) voids non-disclosure provisions limiting disclosure of alleged discriminatory or unfair employment practices unless statutory conditions are met, with penalties for non-compliant provisions. Arbitration cannot bar agency charges (EEOC v. Waffle House, Inc., 534 U.S. 279 (2002)); class waivers are enforceable under Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis, 584 U.S. 497 (2018).",
  "The clause sits in a document that says it is not a contract and can be changed at will, so a court in the Tenth Circuit is likely to refuse enforcement. It expressly covers “harassment” claims without the EFAA carve-out; its blanket confidentiality term conflicts with § 24-34-407; it lacks carve-outs for administrative charges, workers’ compensation, unemployment and FAMLI benefit determinations; and the acknowledgment form conflates receipt of a handbook with contract assent.",
  "All 612 employees; any class or collective wage claim arising from C-1 through C-10 would test the clause.",
  ["Remove §§ 14.2–14.3 from the handbook and, if Oakridge wishes to arbitrate, use a standalone, mutually signed arbitration agreement supported by consideration, with: no unilateral modification (or only prospective modification on notice, not applicable to known claims); EFAA carve-out; agency-charge, workers’ compensation, unemployment and FAMLI carve-outs; a POWR-compliant confidentiality term; and a clear delegation clause.",
   "Keep § 14.1 (internal complaint procedure) in the handbook and replace the Appendix A acknowledgment with a receipt-only form (no covenant or arbitration assent; no witness line needed).",
   "Decide strategy before rollout: an arbitration program rolled out while wage-hour remediation is under way should be coordinated with counsel to avoid claims that it was adopted to defeat known claims."])

f("H-11", "High", "Acquisition transition issues not addressed (Peak Vista and Western Slope employees)",
  "§ 1.1 and § 1.2 (handbook supersedes prior policies); § 12.1 (“deemed to have accepted”); transmittal email (predecessor handbooks “sunsetted”; all employees moved onto the Oakridge handbook)",
  "HFWA successor rule (C.R.S. § 8-13.3-403): employees of a predecessor retain and may use accrued sick leave. Earned vacation under predecessor policies is “wages” that cannot be forfeited (Nieto). FMLA counts predecessor service for a successor in interest (29 C.F.R. § 825.107). Restrictive covenants require individual statutory notice (§ 8-2-113(4)).",
  "The handbook does not say how predecessor PTO/vacation and sick balances were treated, whether predecessor service counts toward eligibility (benefits waiting periods, FMLA, tuition reimbursement, 401(k)), or whether predecessor covenants or arbitration agreements remain in force. If balances were zeroed when the Oakridge handbook was applied (January 15, 2024 and June 3, 2024), the affected employees may have wage claims.",
  "253 employees at the four acquired facilities (Fort Collins 78, Pueblo 62, Grand Junction 58, Durango 55, as reported).",
  ["Obtain the predecessor handbooks and transition records Ms. Kowalski offered, and confirm that every predecessor PTO, vacation and sick balance was either carried over or paid out.",
   "Add a short “Service credit for acquired employees” statement (predecessor service counts for leave eligibility and, as plan documents allow, benefits).",
   "Include predecessor covenants in the non-enforcement notice recommended under C-9."])
EOF
echo ok'
