  "§ 3.1 and § 3.2 (list only race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age, disability and veteran status)",
  "Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act, C.R.S. § 24-34-402, also protects creed, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, ancestry, marital status, genetic information, pregnancy/childbirth and related conditions (§ 24-34-402.3), and — through the CROWN Act (HB 20-1048) — hair texture, hair type and protective hairstyles as part of race; military status is protected under C.R.S. § 28-3-506; lawful off-duty conduct under § 24-34-402.5 (Checklist § 3.1, App. B).",
  "At least seven Colorado classes are missing (creed, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, ancestry, marital status, genetic information), pregnancy is not called out, and hairstyle is absent from both the handbook and our checklist. Genetic information is also federally protected (GINA).",
  "All 612 employees and all applicants.",
  ["Replace the class list in §§ 3.1 and 3.2 with the model language below."],
  lang="“Oakridge prohibits discrimination and harassment based on race (including hair texture, hair type and protective hairstyles), color, religion, creed, sex, pregnancy, childbirth and related conditions, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, national origin, ancestry, age (40 and over), physical or mental disability, marital status, genetic information, veteran or military status, lawful off-duty conduct as protected by Colorado law, or any other status protected by federal, state or local law.”")

f("H-6", "High", "Harassment definition uses the abolished “severe or pervasive” standard; complaint channels are thin",
  "§ 3.2 (hostile environment requires conduct “so severe or pervasive”); § 3.3 (report to supervisor, facility director, or the part-time General Counsel only)",
  "Protecting Opportunities and Workers’ Rights (POWR) Act, SB 23-172 (eff. Aug. 7, 2023): harassment under CADA need not be severe or pervasive (C.R.S. § 24-34-402(1.3)); an employer’s affirmative defense depends on maintaining a program reasonably designed to prevent harassment, deter harassers and protect employees, including a distributed policy, a complaint process with multiple avenues, training, and prompt, reasonable remedial action (C.R.S. § 24-34-402(1.5)). Checklist § 3.3 recommends multiple channels including a hotline.",
  "The “severe or pervasive” language misstates Colorado law and invites employees (and supervisors) to under-report. The only escalation path above a facility director is a part-time General Counsel available in the office Tuesday through Thursday; there is no HR function, no hotline, and no alternative when the facility director is the subject. The General Counsel’s phone number in §§ 3.3 and 14.1 ((719) 555-0134) differs from Ms. Kowalski’s signature block ((719) 555-0148).",
  "All 612 employees; heightened for direct-care staff exposed to resident and family-member conduct.",
  ["Redefine harassment per the POWR Act (unwelcome conduct directed at an employee because of a protected characteristic that is subjectively offensive and objectively offensive to a reasonable person in the same protected class), deleting “severe or pervasive.”",
   "Add at least two additional channels: a corporate HR designee and a 24/7 anonymous hotline or web portal; allow reports to any manager; state that employees need not report to anyone involved in the conduct.",
   "Add a resident-behavior protocol (dementia-related conduct) alongside the existing third-party harassment paragraph, and document annual training for all staff and supervisors."])

f("H-7", "High", "No standalone whistleblower and anti-retaliation policy for a licensed health-care operator",
  "§ 6.2 (safety concerns to supervisor, director or Safety Committee only); § 3.3 and § 6.3 (non-retaliation limited to discrimination and workers’ compensation); § 10.2 (failure to report abuse is misconduct)",
  "Relevant protections include: C.R.S. § 8-2-123 (health-care workers reporting patient-safety information); C.R.S. § 8-14.4-101 et seq. (Public Health Emergency Whistleblower law); C.R.S. § 8-4-120 (wage complaints); C.R.S. §§ 8-13.3-407 and -509 (HFWA and FAMLI); C.R.S. § 24-34-402(1)(e) (CADA); OSHA § 11(c); the federal False Claims Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3730(h), and Colorado’s Medicaid False Claims Act; and mandatory elder-abuse reporting under C.R.S. § 18-6.5-108. Checklist § 6.1 requires a standalone policy with internal and external channels (CDPHE, HCPF, CDLE, EEOC/CCRD, law enforcement).",
  "The handbook has only a general “report safety concerns” statement — exactly the configuration the checklist identifies as insufficient. Several of the checklist’s statutory citations for this section are inaccurate and should not be copied into the handbook (see Section 6).",
  "All 612 employees; particularly the 389 hourly direct-care staff.",
  ["Add a standalone “Reporting Concerns and Non-Retaliation” section covering protected activities (patient/resident safety, abuse/neglect, infection control, staffing, licensing, billing/Medicaid, wage-hour, discrimination, public-health), internal channels including a hotline, external agencies (CDPHE, HCPF, CDLE, CCRD, EEOC, OSHA, law enforcement, the long-term care ombudsman), investigation steps, and discipline for retaliators.",
   "State that nothing in the handbook (including confidentiality and social media rules) restricts reports to government agencies."])

f("H-8", "High", "No accommodation policies (disability, pregnancy, religion, lactation)",
  "No provision; § 6.3 and § 6.4 mention accommodations only in passing",
  "CADA and ADA (disability accommodation and interactive process); C.R.S. § 24-34-402.3 (pregnancy, childbirth and related-condition accommodations, with a written notice-of-rights obligation to new and existing employees); federal Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (eff. June 27, 2023); religious accommodation under Title VII and CADA (Groff v. DeJoy, 600 U.S. 447 (2023), “substantial increased costs” standard); Workplace Accommodations for Nursing Mothers Act, C.R.S. § 8-13.5-101 et seq. (reasonable break time and a private, non-restroom space for up to two years after birth) and the federal PUMP Act.",
  "The handbook has no accommodation request process or pregnancy notice. For a physically demanding, predominantly female caregiving workforce, pregnancy and lifting-restriction accommodations are a frequent source of claims.",
  "All 612 employees.",
  ["Add a consolidated “Reasonable Accommodations” section with an interactive-process description and a single request channel, plus a lactation subsection.",
   "Include the C.R.S. § 24-34-402.3 pregnancy-rights notice in the notices appendix and distribute it with the August 1 handbook."])

f("H-9", "High", "Social media policy bars protected employee speech",
  "§ 13.2 (no post referencing Oakridge, “its residents, staff, services, or operations” or “management” without prior written approval; bar on content “defamatory … toward the Company”); § 13.3",
  "NLRA § 7 protects non-supervisory employees’ concerted discussion of wages, staffing, safety and working conditions, including online, whether or not unionized; overbroad rules are evaluated under Stericycle, Inc., 372 NLRB No. 113 (2023). C.R.S. § 24-34-402.5 limits discipline for lawful off-duty conduct; C.R.S. § 8-2-127 bars requiring access to personal social media accounts; Colorado law protects wage discussions (C.R.S. § 8-5-102).",
  "A prior-approval requirement for any post mentioning co-workers or management would chill core protected activity (for example, CNAs posting about short staffing) and could not lawfully be enforced. The “Communications Department” referenced as the approval body may not exist at Oakridge.",
  "All non-supervisory employees (the large majority of 612).",
  ["Narrow § 13.2 to: (i) resident privacy/PHI and resident images; (ii) genuinely confidential business information and trade secrets; (iii) harassment, threats and discrimination; (iv) speaking on behalf of the Company without authorization; and (v) use of logos to imply endorsement.",
   "Add a savings clause: “Nothing in this policy restricts employees’ rights to discuss wages, hours, staffing or other terms and conditions of employment, to engage in protected concerted activity, or to report concerns to government agencies.”",
   "Confirm who approves official Company posts, and add the § 8-2-127 assurance that Oakridge will not request personal account credentials."])

f("H-10", "High", "Mandatory arbitration clause is likely unenforceable as drafted and conflicts with federal and Colorado law",
  "§ 14.2 (mandatory arbitration, class waiver, confidentiality); § 14.3 (delegation); Appendix A (assent by signing handbook acknowledgment); §§ 1.2 and Appendix A (handbook “not a contract”; Company may modify “at any time … with or without notice”)",
  "An arbitration promise in a handbook that disclaims contractual intent and reserves unilateral modification is illusory (Dumais v. American Golf Corp., 299 F.3d 1216 (10th Cir. 2002)). The Ending Forced Arbitration of Sexual Assault and Sexual Harassment Act, 9 U.S.C. §§ 401–402, lets an employee void pre-dispute arbitration of sexual-harassment and sexual-assault disputes. The POWR Act (C.R.S. § 24-34-407) voids non-disclosure provisions limiting disclosure of alleged discriminatory or unfair employment practices unless statutory conditions are met, with penalties for non-compliant provisions. Arbitration cannot bar agency charges (EEOC v. Waffle House, Inc., 534 U.S. 279 (2002)); class waivers are enforceable under Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis, 584 U.S. 497 (2018).",
  "The clause sits in a document that says it is not a contract and can be changed at will, so a court in the Tenth Circuit is likely to refuse enforcement. It expressly covers “harassment” claims without the EFAA carve-out; its blanket confidentiality term conflicts with § 24-34-407; it lacks carve-outs for administrative charges, workers’ compensation, unemployment and FAMLI benefit determinations; and the acknowledgment form conflates receipt of a handbook with contract assent.",
  "All 612 employees; any class or collective wage claim arising from C-1 through C-10 would test the clause.",
  ["Remove §§ 14.2–14.3 from the handbook and, if Oakridge wishes to arbitrate, use a standalone, mutually signed arbitration agreement supported by consideration, with: no unilateral modification (or only prospective modification on notice, not applicable to known claims); EFAA carve-out; agency-charge, workers’ compensation, unemployment and FAMLI carve-outs; a POWR-compliant confidentiality term; and a clear delegation clause.",
   "Keep § 14.1 (internal complaint procedure) in the handbook and replace the Appendix A acknowledgment with a receipt-only form (no covenant or arbitration assent; no witness line needed).",
   "Decide strategy before rollout: an arbitration program rolled out while wage-hour remediation is under way should be coordinated with counsel to avoid claims that it was adopted to defeat known claims."])

f("H-11", "High", "Acquisition transition issues not addressed (Peak Vista and Western Slope employees)",
  "§ 1.1 and § 1.2 (handbook supersedes prior policies); § 12.1 (“deemed to have accepted”); transmittal email (predecessor handbooks “sunsetted”; all employees moved onto the Oakridge handbook)",
  "HFWA successor rule (C.R.S. § 8-13.3-403): employees of a predecessor retain and may use accrued sick leave. Earned vacation under predecessor policies is “wages” that cannot be forfeited (Nieto). FMLA counts predecessor service for a successor in interest (29 C.F.R. § 825.107). Restrictive covenants require individual statutory notice (§ 8-2-113(4)).",
  "The handbook does not say how predecessor PTO/vacation and sick balances were treated, whether predecessor service counts toward eligibility (benefits waiting periods, FMLA, tuition reimbursement, 401(k)), or whether predecessor covenants or arbitration agreements remain in force. If balances were zeroed when the Oakridge handbook was applied (January 15, 2024 and June 3, 2024), the affected employees may have wage claims.",
  "253 employees at the four acquired facilities (Fort Collins 78, Pueblo 62, Grand Junction 58, Durango 55, as reported).",
  ["Obtain the predecessor handbooks and transition records Ms. Kowalski offered, and confirm that every predecessor PTO, vacation and sick balance was either carried over or paid out.",
   "Add a short “Service credit for acquired employees” statement (predecessor service counts for leave eligibility and, as plan documents allow, benefits).",
   "Include predecessor covenants in the non-enforcement notice recommended under C-9."])

input.command:
S=/home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/sbx.sh; R=/home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/vendor/harvey-labs/results/employment-labor/compare-employee-handbook-against-state-requirements/claude-code-session/20261016-032126; $S $R 'cat > /workspace/build/p3c.py <<"EOF"
f("M-1", "Medium", "Salaried non-exempt pay and regular-rate rules not described",
  "§ 2.2 (salaried non-exempt employees “remain eligible for overtime”); § 4.3; § 4.5 (timekeeping)",
  "COMPS Order #39, Rule 1.8: a non-exempt employee’s salary is presumed to compensate no more than 40 hours per week; Colorado does not permit the federal “fluctuating workweek” half-time method; the regular rate includes shift differentials and non-discretionary bonuses. Records must capture daily hours to support daily overtime (Checklist § 1.2).",
  "With 75 salaried non-exempt employees, a payroll method that pays half-time for overtime or divides salary by all hours worked would under-pay overtime under Colorado law. The handbook does not commit to recording daily hours, meal and rest periods.",
  "75 salaried non-exempt employees; all 464 non-exempt for regular-rate and timekeeping.",
  ["Confirm with Pinnacle how salaried non-exempt overtime is calculated; add a sentence that salary covers 40 hours and overtime is paid at 1.5× the hourly equivalent of salary.",
   "Amend § 4.5 to require recording of daily start/stop times, meal periods and missed rest breaks."], act=True)

f("M-2", "Medium", "Pay-deduction section incomplete; property-return deduction not limited",
  "§ 4.6 (deductions); § 4.7 (deduction for unreturned property)",
  "FAMLI requires the employee premium deduction (C.R.S. § 8-13.3-507). Wage deductions are permitted only as listed in C.R.S. § 8-4-105 (including written authorization requirements) and cannot reduce a non-exempt employee’s pay below the applicable minimum wage or delay final pay.",
  "The required-deduction list omits FAMLI. The property-return clause is open-ended (“to the extent permitted”) without describing the conditions, which encourages facility-level practices that violate § 8-4-105.",
  "All 612 employees (FAMLI); separating employees (property).",
  ["Add FAMLI to required deductions; add HSA/FSA or other voluntary deductions as applicable.",
   "Limit property deductions to items covered by a signed written authorization and the conditions of § 8-4-105, and state they will not delay final pay or reduce wages below minimum wage."])

f("M-3", "Medium", "Required notices not included in the handbook; pay statement and wage notice content not described",
  "§ 2.3 (payroll); handbook has no notices appendix",
  "COMPS Order #39, Rule 7: employers must post the COMPS poster and, where an employee handbook is provided, include the COMPS Order or poster in the handbook. Pay statements must itemize gross wages, deductions, net pay, hours worked (non-exempt), the pay period and employer identification (C.R.S. § 8-4-103(4)). Colorado also requires written notice of pay rate, payday and deductions at hire (Checklist § 7.1) and the posting of HFWA, FAMLI, CADA, pregnancy-accommodation and “Notice of Paydays” information (Checklist § 7.2).",
  "There is no notices appendix and no description of the itemized pay statement. The biweekly Friday payday (six days after the Saturday period close) is permissible and correctly stated.",
  "All 612 employees.",
  ["Add an appendix reproducing the current COMPS poster and the HFWA, FAMLI and pregnancy-accommodation notices (Spanish versions available from CDLE should be distributed where employees are more comfortable reading Spanish).",
   "Add a sentence to § 2.3 describing the itemized pay statement and the hire-date wage notice."])

f("M-4", "Medium", "External complaint section names only the EEOC, not the Colorado Civil Rights Division",
  "§ 3.3 (External Reporting)",
  "Charges under CADA are filed with the Colorado Civil Rights Division within 300 days (C.R.S. § 24-34-403, as amended by HB 22-1367); the EEOC and CCRD cross-file under a worksharing agreement (Checklist § 3.2).",
  "Employees are told only of the EEOC. This is incomplete and suggests unfamiliarity with state law.",
  "All 612 employees.",
  ["Add the CCRD (Colorado Civil Rights Division, 1560 Broadway, Suite 825, Denver, CO 80202; ccrd.colorado.gov — verify current contact information before publication) and the 300-day filing period for both agencies."])

f("M-5", "Medium", "Pay transparency and wage-discussion protections absent; confidentiality language could be read to bar wage discussions",
  "§ 4.1 (wage administration); § 10.4 (confidentiality of “employee personnel information” and “financial data”)",
  "Equal Pay for Equal Work Act, C.R.S. § 8-5-101 et seq.: no pay differentials based on sex (or sex plus another protected status) for substantially similar work; no wage-history inquiries; employees may not be prohibited from discussing or disclosing their wages; job postings must include a good-faith pay range and a general description of benefits; employers must announce promotional and job opportunities and, since 2024, provide post-selection and career-progression information (SB 23-105).",
  "The handbook is silent on these obligations and its confidentiality clause is broad enough to chill wage discussions (also an NLRA issue).",
  "All 612 employees; applicants.",
  ["Add a brief “Pay Equity and Transparency” paragraph to § 4.1 and a carve-out in § 10.4 clarifying that employees may discuss their own wages and working conditions."])

f("M-6", "Medium", "Progressive discipline language undercuts the at-will disclaimer",
  "§ 11.1 (mandatory “will” sequence; “Employees will be given the opportunity to improve performance before termination, except in cases of gross misconduct”); § 1.3; § 2.1 (introductory period)",
  "Colorado enforces at-will employment, but handbook procedures phrased as mandatory can create an implied contract or support promissory estoppel (Continental Air Lines, Inc. v. Keenan, 731 P.2d 708 (Colo. 1987)); a clear and conspicuous disclaimer generally defeats such claims only if the handbook does not contradict it (Checklist § 7.5).",
  "The reservation paragraph is helpful, but the sentence promising an opportunity to improve except for “gross misconduct” is a specific promise that a plaintiff will cite, and the steps are stated as obligations (“will issue,” “will be terminated”). Section 11.1 also requires General Counsel approval of every termination, which may delay final pay (C-8).",
  "All 612 employees.",
  ["Delete the “Employees will be given the opportunity to improve” sentence.",
   "Recast the steps as permissive (“may include”), add an express cross-reference to § 1.3, and add that the introductory period and progressive discipline do not create a right to any particular process.",
   "Allow a designated HR or operations leader to approve terminations when the General Counsel is unavailable."])

f("M-7", "Medium", "Employee non-solicit, one-sided remedies and tuition repayment need Colorado-specific limits",
  "§ 12.3 (12-month non-solicit of employees, all employees); § 12.4 (Company recovers fees; employee “acknowledges” irreparable harm; judicial reformation); § 8.5 (tuition reimbursement repayment “for a specified period”)",
  "C.R.S. § 8-2-113(2)(a) voids covenants restricting a worker’s right to receive compensation for labor; employee non-solicits are not an enumerated exception and their enforceability against low-wage workers is uncertain. § 8-2-113(8) awards fees to workers harmed by void covenants. Training-cost repayment is permitted only within § 8-2-113(3) (education distinct from normal on-the-job training; workers employed less than two years), and any repayment by deduction must comply with § 8-4-105.",
  "Applying a no-poach covenant to caregivers is of doubtful enforceability and, if characterized as a restraint on labor, carries the same § 8-2-113(8) penalty exposure. The tuition provision leaves the repayment period unspecified.",
  "All 612 employees (§ 12.3); full-time employees using tuition reimbursement (§ 8.5).",
  ["Remove § 12.3 from the handbook; if desired, include a narrowly drawn employee non-solicit only in the standalone agreements for eligible management employees.",
   "Delete the one-sided fee and irreparable-harm language from the handbook.",
   "Replace the open-ended tuition clause with a signed repayment agreement that fixes a period of not more than two years, prorates repayment, and limits it to education distinct from normal job training."])

f("M-8", "Medium", "Colorado-specific leaves omitted (domestic violence leave; crime-victim leave)",
  "§ 7 (Leaves of Absence)",
  "C.R.S. § 24-34-402.7: employers with 50 or more employees must permit eligible employees up to three working days of leave (paid or unpaid) in any 12-month period to address domestic abuse, stalking, sexual assault or other crimes related to domestic violence. C.R.S. § 24-4.1-303(8): employers may not penalize crime victims for attending criminal proceedings.",
  "Neither leave is mentioned; HFWA also covers safe-leave reasons (C-7).",
  "All 612 employees.",
  ["Add a “Domestic Violence and Crime Victim Leave” subsection describing the three-day entitlement, notice and confidentiality, and its interaction with HFWA and FAMLI safe leave."])

f("M-9", "Medium", "Remote work guidelines described in transmittal are missing from the handbook provided",
  "Transmittal (March 14, 2025 update “added … remote work guidelines”); handbook Sections 1–14 contain no remote work policy",
  "Any remote or hybrid arrangement for non-exempt staff must preserve COMPS timekeeping, meal/rest and overtime compliance; HIPAA security rules apply to remote access to PHI.",
  "Either the remote work section was omitted from the copy we received or it was never inserted. The version distributed on August 1 must be the version reviewed.",
  "Administrative and corporate staff (number unknown).",
  ["Send us the remote work section (or confirm none exists) so it can be reviewed before distribution; implement version control for the August 1 release."])

f("L-1", "Low", "Personnel file access process not described",
  "§ 11.2 (“in accordance with applicable Colorado law”)",
  "C.R.S. § 8-2-129: current employees may inspect and obtain a copy of their personnel file at least annually, and former employees once after termination; the employer may require inspection at its office in the presence of an employer representative (Checklist § 7.3).",
  "The right is referenced but not explained (process and timing).",
  "All 612 employees; former employees.",
  ["State the request process (written request to facility HR), the response timeframe, and the annual/one-time post-termination inspection rights."])

f("L-2", "Low", "Factual inaccuracies and stale details in the handbook",
  "§ 1.1 (welcome letter); §§ 3.3, 14.1 (contact details); § 13 (“Communications Department”); § 10.4 (“Privacy Officer”)",
  "Accuracy and internal consistency (no specific statute).",
  "The welcome letter states that Peak Vista brought the “Pueblo and Denver” facilities; per the census and transmittal, Peak Vista added Fort Collins and Pueblo, and Denver is an original facility. It also describes Oakridge as beginning with “a single community,” whereas the transmittal describes three original facilities. The General Counsel phone number appears to be wrong (see H-6). The Communications Department and Privacy Officer are referenced but not identified.",
  "All 612 employees.",
  ["Correct the acquisition history, replace named individuals with titles and a shared HR mailbox, and identify the Privacy Officer and the social media approver by title."])

f("L-3", "Low", "Jury duty, voting and military leave details",
  "§ 7.1 (jury: regular pay up to three days “per calendar year,” based on scheduled hours); § 7.5 (voting); § 7.3 (military)",
  "C.R.S. § 13-71-126 requires regular wages (up to $50/day unless otherwise agreed) for the first three days of juror service for regular, part-time, temporary and casual employees, and § 13-71-134 bars penalizing jurors. C.R.S. § 1-7-102 (voting leave) — handbook is compliant. C.R.S. § 28-3-609 provides up to 15 days per year of leave for Colorado-resident National Guard and reserve training with reinstatement.",
  "Jury pay should be tied to each period of service rather than a calendar-year cap, and should state that temporary and part-time employees are covered. Military leave should mention the state 15-day training leave.",
  "Employees summoned for jury service or in the Guard/reserves.",
  ["Clarify § 7.1 and add a sentence on Colorado military training leave to § 7.3; § 7.5 may remain, adding that the employer will grant leave at the beginning or end of the shift if the employee so requests."])

f("L-4", "Low", "Drug and alcohol policy clarifications",
  "§ 6.4 (Drug-Free Workplace)",
  "Colorado’s lawful off-duty statute does not protect marijuana use (Coats v. Dish Network, LLC, 2015 CO 44); Colorado’s Natural Medicine Health Act likewise permits employers to maintain drug-free workplace policies. The federal Drug-Free Workplace Act applies only to federal contractors and grantees. Prescription disclosures are subject to ADA/CADA confidentiality.",
  "The policy is substantively sound but should state expressly that lawful-under-state-law marijuana and natural medicine are prohibited on duty and may be tested for, and that medication disclosures are kept confidential and handled through the accommodation process.",
  "Direct-care and safety-sensitive staff.",
  ["Add marijuana/natural-medicine and confidentiality sentences; confirm whether Oakridge is a covered federal contractor or grantee before citing the Drug-Free Workplace Act."])

f("L-5", "Low", "FMLA section technical updates",
  "§ 9.1–9.3",
  "29 C.F.R. § 825.300(a)(3): where an employer has a handbook, the FMLA general notice content must be included. Successor-in-interest service counts toward eligibility (29 C.F.R. § 825.107). Substitution of paid leave and concurrency should be explained.",
  "The section is generally accurate but omits the general-notice items on prohibited acts and enforcement (DOL complaint rights), paid-leave substitution, and concurrency with FAMLI, HFWA/PTO and workers’ compensation.",
  "Employees eligible for FMLA.",
  ["Add the missing general-notice content and a concurrency paragraph cross-referencing the new FAMLI section."])
EOF
echo ok'
